items.sentence: He is senior than me in the department.
answers: He is senior to me in the department.
items.explanation: Comparatives borrowed from Latin (senior, junior, superior, inferior, prior) take 'to', not 'than'.

items.sentence: We will discuss about the proposal at tomorrow's meeting.
answers: We will discuss the proposal at tomorrow's meeting.
items.explanation: 'Discuss' is a transitive verb and takes a direct object; 'about' is not used after it (compare 'a discussion about').

items.sentence: Please return back the library books by Friday.
answers: Please return the library books by Friday.
items.explanation: 'Return' already means 'give or come back', so 'back' is redundant.

items.sentence: One of my friend has joined the Foreign Service.
answers: One of my friends has joined the Foreign Service.
items.explanation: 'One of' picks one member from a group, so the noun after it must be plural; the verb stays singular to agree with 'one'.

items.sentence: She has been teaching at this college since two years.
answers: She has been teaching at this college for two years.
items.explanation: 'For' is used with a period of time (two years); 'since' is used with a point in time (since 2023).

items.sentence: The childrens toys were scattered across the floor.
answers: The children's toys were scattered across the floor.
items.explanation: A plural noun that does not end in -s forms its possessive with apostrophe + s: children's.

items.sentence: Each of the candidates have submitted an application.
answers: Each of the candidates has submitted an application.
items.explanation: 'Each' is singular, so it takes a singular verb even when followed by 'of' + plural noun.

items.sentence: Neither the minister nor his advisers was available for comment.
answers: Neither the minister nor his advisers were available for comment.
items.explanation: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject; 'advisers' is plural, so 'were'.

items.sentence: If it will rain tomorrow, the match will be postponed.
answers: If it rains tomorrow, the match will be postponed.
items.explanation: In a first conditional the if-clause takes the present simple, not 'will', even when it refers to the future.

items.sentence: If the guard had been alert, the robbery would not take place.
answers: If the guard had been alert, the robbery would not have taken place.
items.explanation: An unreal past condition (had + past participle) needs 'would have' + past participle in the main clause.

items.sentence: The company has raised it's prices again.
answers: The company has raised its prices again.
items.explanation: 'Its' is the possessive pronoun and has no apostrophe; 'it's' means 'it is' or 'it has'.

items.sentence: The witness did not say nothing to the police.
answers: The witness did not say anything to the police.
The witness said nothing to the police.
items.explanation: Two negatives ('not' and 'nothing') should not be combined in standard English; use 'not ... anything' or 'nothing' alone.

items.sentence: She can speak Pashto fluently, isn't it?
answers: She can speak Pashto fluently, can't she?
items.explanation: A question tag repeats the auxiliary and subject of the statement in the opposite polarity: 'She can ..., can't she?' ('isn't it' is not a universal tag).

items.sentence: I look forward to meet you at the seminar.
answers: I look forward to meeting you at the seminar.
items.explanation: In 'look forward to', 'to' is a preposition, so it is followed by the -ing form, not the base verb.

items.sentence: My teacher gave me an advice that changed my career.
answers: My teacher gave me advice that changed my career.
My teacher gave me a piece of advice that changed my career.
My teacher gave me some advice that changed my career.
items.explanation: 'Advice' is uncountable and cannot take 'a/an'; use it alone or say 'a piece of advice'.

items.sentence: The bus was late, we missed the first lecture.
answers: The bus was late; we missed the first lecture.
The bus was late. We missed the first lecture.
The bus was late, so we missed the first lecture.
items.explanation: Two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone; use a semicolon, a full stop, or a comma with a conjunction.

items.sentence: She is an university lecturer in Hyderabad.
answers: She is a university lecturer in Hyderabad.
items.explanation: The choice of 'a' or 'an' depends on sound: 'university' begins with a 'yoo' (consonant) sound, so it takes 'a'.

items.sentence: The Indus is longest river in Pakistan.
answers: The Indus is the longest river in Pakistan.
items.explanation: A superlative adjective before a noun normally takes the definite article: 'the longest'.

items.sentence: Between you and I, the scheme will not succeed.
answers: Between you and me, the scheme will not succeed.
items.explanation: A pronoun that is the object of a preposition ('between') must be in the object form: 'me', not 'I'.

items.sentence: Whom do you think will win the election?
answers: Who do you think will win the election?
items.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of 'will win' ('do you think' is only inserted), so the subject form 'who' is required.

items.sentence: She teaches english at a college in Multan.
answers: She teaches English at a college in Multan.
items.explanation: Names of languages are proper nouns and always begin with a capital letter.

items.sentence: He is enough old to vote in the general election.
answers: He is old enough to vote in the general election.
items.explanation: 'Enough' comes after an adjective or adverb ('old enough') but before a noun ('enough money').

items.sentence: He enjoys reading, travelling and to write poetry.
answers: He enjoys reading, travelling and writing poetry.
items.explanation: Items in a list should share the same grammatical form; the other items are gerunds, so 'writing'.

items.sentence: Our teacher told us that the earth moved round the sun.
answers: Our teacher told us that the earth moves round the sun.
items.explanation: A universal or permanent truth stays in the present tense even after a past reporting verb.

items.sentence: When we reached the station, the train already left.
answers: When we reached the station, the train had already left.
items.explanation: Of two past actions, the one completed earlier takes the past perfect: the train 'had already left' before we reached.

items.sentence: The plan was sound, however, it was never implemented.
answers: The plan was sound; however, it was never implemented.
The plan was sound. However, it was never implemented.
items.explanation: 'However' joining two independent clauses is not a conjunction; it needs a semicolon (or full stop) before it and a comma after it.

items.sentence: I have met him at the conference yesterday.
answers: I met him at the conference yesterday.
items.explanation: The present perfect is not used with a finished past time such as 'yesterday'; use the past simple.

items.sentence: Unless you do not work hard, you will fail.
answers: Unless you work hard, you will fail.
items.explanation: 'Unless' already means 'if not', so it should not be followed by another 'not'.

items.sentence: No sooner had the minister arrived when the protest began.
answers: No sooner had the minister arrived than the protest began.
items.explanation: 'No sooner' is a comparative form and pairs with 'than', not 'when'.

items.sentence: The furniture in these offices are imported.
answers: The furniture in these offices is imported.
items.explanation: 'Furniture' is uncountable and takes a singular verb; the plural 'offices' in the phrase does not change the subject.

items.sentence: He asked me why I was late?
answers: He asked me why I was late.
items.explanation: An indirect (reported) question is a statement and ends with a full stop, not a question mark.

items.sentence: My cousin sister is getting married next month.
answers: My cousin is getting married next month.
items.explanation: 'Cousin' already covers both sexes; 'cousin sister' is not standard English.

items.sentence: She is married with a civil servant.
answers: She is married to a civil servant.
items.explanation: One is 'married to' a person in standard English, not 'married with'.

items.sentence: Most people prefer tea than coffee in winter.
answers: Most people prefer tea to coffee in winter.
items.explanation: 'Prefer' one thing 'to' another; 'than' is wrong here because 'prefer' is not a comparative.

items.sentence: We congratulated him for his success in the exam.
answers: We congratulated him on his success in the exam.
items.explanation: In standard British English one congratulates someone 'on' an achievement.

items.sentence: My father who is a retired judge lives in Peshawar.
answers: My father, who is a retired judge, lives in Peshawar.
items.explanation: A person has only one father, so the clause adds extra information (non-defining) and must be enclosed in commas.

items.sentence: The police has arrested three suspects.
answers: The police have arrested three suspects.
items.explanation: 'Police' is always treated as plural in English and takes a plural verb.

items.sentence: The number of road accidents have increased this year.
answers: The number of road accidents has increased this year.
items.explanation: The subject is 'the number', which is singular; contrast 'a number of', which means 'several' and takes a plural verb.

items.sentence: She sang the national anthem very sweet.
answers: She sang the national anthem very sweetly.
items.explanation: A word describing how an action is done must be an adverb: 'sang sweetly'.

items.sentence: This road is more wider than the old one.
answers: This road is wider than the old one.
items.explanation: 'Wider' is already comparative; adding 'more' doubles the comparison.

items.sentence: Bring the following items, a pen, a calculator and your admit card.
answers: Bring the following items: a pen, a calculator and your admit card.
items.explanation: A colon, not a comma, introduces a list after a complete clause such as 'Bring the following items'.

items.sentence: Karachi is larger than any city in Pakistan.
answers: Karachi is larger than any other city in Pakistan.
items.explanation: When comparing something with the group it belongs to, add 'other'; otherwise Karachi is compared with itself.

items.sentence: Although he was unwell, but he attended the meeting.
answers: Although he was unwell, he attended the meeting.
items.explanation: 'Although' already links the clauses; adding 'but' uses two conjunctions for one link.

items.sentence: Despite of the heavy rain, the match continued.
answers: Despite the heavy rain, the match continued.
In spite of the heavy rain, the match continued.
items.explanation: 'Despite' is never followed by 'of'; the alternative form is 'in spite of'.

items.sentence: There were less candidates this year than last year.
answers: There were fewer candidates this year than last year.
items.explanation: 'Fewer' is used with plural countable nouns (candidates); 'less' is used with uncountable nouns (less water).

items.sentence: The final decision is your's to make.
answers: The final decision is yours to make.
items.explanation: Possessive pronouns such as yours, hers, ours and theirs never take an apostrophe.

items.sentence: The suspect avoided to answer the question.
answers: The suspect avoided answering the question.
items.explanation: 'Avoid' is followed by the -ing form, not the to-infinitive (like 'deny', 'enjoy', 'finish').

items.sentence: The teacher made him to apologise.
answers: The teacher made him apologise.
items.explanation: In the active voice, 'make' and 'let' are followed by object + infinitive without 'to'.

items.sentence: Can you tell me where does he live?
answers: Can you tell me where he lives?
items.explanation: An indirect question inside a sentence uses statement word order (subject + verb), without 'do/does'.

items.sentence: I didn't went to the office yesterday.
answers: I didn't go to the office yesterday.
items.explanation: After 'did/didn't' the main verb takes its base form; the past is shown by 'did' alone.

items.sentence: The students who passed the written test, will be called for interview.
answers: The students who passed the written test will be called for interview.
items.explanation: A defining clause is part of the subject; no comma should separate the subject from its verb.

items.sentence: Ali, as well as his brothers, are coming to dinner.
answers: Ali, as well as his brothers, is coming to dinner.
items.explanation: Phrases introduced by 'as well as' or 'along with' do not change the subject; the verb agrees with 'Ali'.

items.sentence: She is elder than her brother.
answers: She is older than her brother.
items.explanation: 'Elder' is used only before a noun or as 'the elder'; it is not followed by 'than', which requires 'older'.

items.sentence: The criteria for selection was announced last week.
answers: The criteria for selection were announced last week.
items.explanation: 'Criteria' is the plural of 'criterion' and takes a plural verb.

items.sentence: It is high time we leave for the airport.
answers: It is high time we left for the airport.
items.explanation: 'It is (high) time' + subject is followed by the past simple, though the meaning is present.

items.sentence: The patient was died before the ambulance arrived.
answers: The patient had died before the ambulance arrived.
The patient died before the ambulance arrived.
items.explanation: 'Die' is intransitive and cannot be used in the passive; use 'died' or, for the earlier action, 'had died'.

items.sentence: Prices have raised sharply this year.
answers: Prices have risen sharply this year.
items.explanation: 'Rise' (rose, risen) is intransitive; 'raise' needs an object (raise prices).

items.sentence: The book which I bought it yesterday is missing.
answers: The book which I bought yesterday is missing.
items.explanation: The relative pronoun 'which' is already the object of 'bought', so the extra 'it' must be removed.

items.sentence: He went to the market for buying vegetables.
answers: He went to the market to buy vegetables.
items.explanation: Purpose after a verb of motion is expressed by the to-infinitive, not 'for' + -ing.

items.sentence: I am agree with your proposal.
answers: I agree with your proposal.
items.explanation: 'Agree' is a verb, not an adjective, so it does not take 'am'.

items.sentence: His knowledge of languages and international relations aid him in his work.
answers: His knowledge of languages and international relations aids him in his work.
items.explanation: The subject is 'knowledge' (singular); 'of languages and international relations' only describes it, so the verb is 'aids'.

items.sentence: The ambassador, with his family and staff, invite you to a reception at the embassy on Tuesday afternoon.
answers: The ambassador, with his family and staff, invites you to a reception at the embassy on Tuesday afternoon.
items.explanation: A phrase introduced by 'with', 'as well as' or 'along with' does not change the subject. 'The ambassador' is singular, so the verb is 'invites'.

items.sentence: This year, he will sit in the CSS examination.
answers: This year, he will sit for the CSS examination.
This year, he will sit the CSS examination.
items.explanation: We 'sit an examination' (British) or 'sit for an examination'; 'sit in' means to attend as an observer.

items.sentence: The Chief Executive will let us know whether or not he can attend the meeting.
answers: The Chief Executive will let us know whether he can attend the meeting.
items.explanation: 'Whether' already covers both possibilities, so 'or not' is redundant here; the usual model answer drops it.

items.sentence: When he came back from vacation, Aslam and me plan to look for another apartment.
answers: When he comes back from vacation, Aslam and I plan to look for another apartment.
When he came back from vacation, Aslam and I planned to look for another apartment.
items.explanation: 'Aslam and I' is the subject, so the subject pronoun 'I' is needed. The tenses must also match: 'comes … plan' (future plan) or 'came … planned' (past).

items.sentence: If some of you make a noise, they shall be punished.
answers: If any of you make a noise, you will be punished.
If some of you make a noise, you will be punished.
If any of you makes a noise, you will be punished.
items.explanation: The sentence addresses 'you', so the second clause must also use 'you', not 'they'. 'Any of you' is the more natural choice in a condition.

items.sentence: He came to me to enquire what is the salary attached to the appointment.
answers: He came to me to enquire what the salary attached to the appointment was.
He came to me to enquire what the salary attached to the appointment is.
items.explanation: In an indirect question the subject comes before the verb ('what the salary … was'), and after a past reporting verb the tense usually moves back.

items.sentence: I am too tired that I do not hunt words and idioms in my English book.
answers: I am so tired that I cannot hunt for words and idioms in my English book.
I am too tired to hunt for words and idioms in my English book.
items.explanation: 'Too' is followed by an infinitive ('too tired to hunt'); 'so' is followed by a 'that' clause ('so tired that I cannot'). 'Hunt for' is the correct verb pattern.

items.sentence: Chewing slowly, the pepperoni pizza tasted delicious.
answers: Chewing slowly, I found the pepperoni pizza delicious.
As I chewed slowly, the pepperoni pizza tasted delicious.
items.explanation: The opening phrase must describe the subject that follows it. A pizza cannot chew, so the subject has to be the person eating.

items.sentence: Kicking and screaming, the exasperated father dragged his toddler out of the grocery store.
answers: The exasperated father dragged his kicking and screaming toddler out of the grocery store.
The exasperated father dragged his toddler, kicking and screaming, out of the grocery store.
items.explanation: As written, the father is kicking and screaming. Place the modifier next to the toddler, who is doing it.

items.sentence: A young girl in the corner, holding a red balloon.
answers: A young girl was standing in the corner, holding a red balloon.
A young girl in the corner was holding a red balloon.
items.explanation: There is no main verb, so this is a fragment. Add a finite verb such as 'was standing' or 'was holding'.

items.sentence: Whom do you like more?
answers: Whom do you like better?
Which do you like better?
items.explanation: When choosing between two, the idiom is 'like better'. The usual model answer keeps the object pronoun 'whom'.

items.sentence: He ordered a meal from the restaurant that was high in protein.
answers: He ordered a meal that was high in protein from the restaurant.
From the restaurant, he ordered a meal that was high in protein.
He ordered a high-protein meal from the restaurant.
items.explanation: 'That was high in protein' now seems to describe the restaurant. Put it next to 'meal'.

items.sentence: My favorite pizza topping is mushrooms they are really tasty I also like pizza with olives.
answers: My favorite pizza topping is mushrooms; they are really tasty. I also like pizza with olives.
My favorite pizza topping is mushrooms. They are really tasty. I also like pizza with olives.
items.explanation: Three independent clauses are run together. Separate them with full stops or a semicolon.

items.sentence: The group asked to hear the report that Shirley and me prepared.
answers: The group asked to hear the report that Shirley and I prepared.
items.explanation: 'Shirley and I' is the subject of 'prepared', so the subject pronoun 'I' is required.

items.sentence: I managed finishing the painting.
answers: I managed to finish the painting.
items.explanation: 'Manage' is followed by a to-infinitive, not a gerund.

items.sentence: Having been perpetuated for centuries the systemic inequalities and discriminatory policies of the government which has been institutionalized, are a form of structural violence that affect marginalized communities.
answers: Having been perpetuated for centuries, the systemic inequalities and discriminatory policies of the government, which have been institutionalized, are a form of structural violence that affects marginalized communities.
items.explanation: Put a comma after the opening phrase; the relative clause refers to the plural 'inequalities and policies', so 'which have been', enclosed in commas; and 'structural violence' takes 'affects'.

items.sentence: We cleaned all the kitchen while our parents were out to dinner.
answers: We cleaned the whole kitchen while our parents were out to dinner.
We cleaned the whole kitchen while our parents were out for dinner.
We cleaned the entire kitchen while our parents were out to dinner.
items.explanation: With a singular countable noun, use 'the whole' or 'the entire', not 'all the'.

items.sentence: If I'm stressed out about something, I tend to have problem to fall asleep.
answers: If I'm stressed out about something, I tend to have trouble falling asleep.
If I'm stressed out about something, I tend to have a problem falling asleep.
If I'm stressed out about something, I tend to have problems falling asleep.
items.explanation: The pattern is 'have trouble/a problem + -ing', and countable 'problem' needs an article or plural.

items.sentence: If I will be in Lahore, I will contact to you.
answers: If I am in Lahore, I will contact you.
items.explanation: The if-clause of a first conditional takes the present tense ('If I am'), and 'contact' takes a direct object without 'to'.

items.sentence: The cultural globalization —it is a phenomenon that has been driven by technological advancements and economic integration —is a threat to local cultures.
answers: Cultural globalization—a phenomenon that has been driven by technological advancements and economic integration—is a threat to local cultures.
Cultural globalization, a phenomenon that has been driven by technological advancements and economic integration, is a threat to local cultures.
items.explanation: The words between dashes should be an appositive describing the subject ('a phenomenon …'), not a new clause with 'it is'. An abstract noun used generally takes no article.

items.sentence: The impact of cybertechnology on modern society is being studied by researchers, who has found that it has both positive and negative effects.
answers: The impact of cybertechnology on modern society is being studied by researchers, who have found that it has both positive and negative effects.
items.explanation: 'Who' refers to 'researchers' (plural), so the verb is 'have found'.

items.sentence: The experimental novel —which blends elements of poetry and prose —is a challenge to traditional notions of storytelling and narrative structure, but it will have been widely accepted by the time it is recognized as a masterpiece.
answers: The experimental novel—which blends elements of poetry and prose—is a challenge to traditional notions of storytelling and narrative structure, but it will be widely accepted by the time it is recognized as a masterpiece.
items.explanation: The suggested model answer uses the simple future ('will be widely accepted'): the future perfect implies acceptance completed before recognition, which does not fit the logic of the sentence. Dashes take no space before them.

items.sentence: The honor killings that having been perpetuate by the societies are exacting a deadly toll on the vulnerable individuals which are exacerbating the excruciating norms more.
answers: The honor killings that have been perpetuated by society are exacting a deadly toll on vulnerable individuals and are further exacerbating oppressive norms.
The honor killings that have been perpetuated by societies are exacting a deadly toll on vulnerable individuals and are further exacerbating the oppressive norms.
items.explanation: The relative clause needs a finite verb ('have been perpetuated'). 'Which are exacerbating' wrongly refers to the individuals, and 'more' is misplaced; the model answer links the two ideas with 'and are further exacerbating'.

items.sentence: It is a fact that I almost drowned makes me very careful about water safety whenever I go swimming.
answers: The fact that I almost drowned makes me very careful about water safety whenever I go swimming.
items.explanation: The subject of 'makes' is the noun phrase 'The fact that I almost drowned'; 'It is a fact that' creates a second main verb.

items.sentence: The amount they receive in wages is greater than twenty years ago.
answers: The amount they receive in wages is greater than it was twenty years ago.
items.explanation: The comparison needs a matching clause: the amount now is greater than it was then.

items.sentence: Playing a game regularly is better than to read books always.
answers: Playing a game regularly is better than reading books all the time.
Playing a game regularly is better than always reading books.
items.explanation: Compared items must have the same form: gerund with gerund ('playing … reading'). 'Always' sits more naturally before the verb or as 'all the time'.

items.sentence: It is one of the best speeches that ever been made in the General Assembly.
answers: It is one of the best speeches that have ever been made in the General Assembly.
It is one of the best speeches that has ever been made in the General Assembly.
items.explanation: The passive perfect needs 'have/has': 'that have ever been made'. Strictly, 'that' refers to 'speeches', so 'have' is preferred.

items.sentence: Ever since they had heard about the burglaries in neighbourhood they kept on the light all the time and close all the doors and the windows very carefully.
answers: Ever since they heard about the burglaries in the neighbourhood, they have kept the lights on all the time and have closed all the doors and windows very carefully.
Ever since they heard about the burglaries in the neighbourhood, they have kept the lights on all the time and closed all the doors and windows very carefully.
items.explanation: 'Ever since' + simple past is followed by the present perfect in the main clause. 'The neighbourhood' needs the article, 'kept the lights on' is the natural order, and the verbs must be parallel.

items.sentence: When Susan realised that all of her bottles of the mail polish dries out she decides to keep them for decoration.
answers: When Susan realised that all of her bottles of nail polish had dried out, she decided to keep them for decoration.
items.explanation: After the past 'realised', the earlier action takes the past perfect ('had dried out') and the main verb stays in the past ('decided'). 'Nail polish' takes no article.

items.sentence: It was late in night and a boy rode his bike along the path when suddenly he stopped in shock as his head lamp was not working anymore.
answers: It was late at night and a boy was riding his bike along the path when suddenly he stopped in shock as his head lamp was not working any more.
It was late at night and a boy was riding his bike along the path when suddenly he stopped in shock as his head lamp was not working anymore.
items.explanation: The idiom is 'late at night'. The background action interrupted by 'when' takes the past continuous ('was riding').

items.sentence: The girl told the conductor that she lost her train ticket and knew not how she would get home.
answers: The girl told the conductor that she had lost her train ticket and did not know how she would get home.
items.explanation: The earlier action takes the past perfect ('had lost'), and modern English forms the negative with 'did not know', not 'knew not'.

items.sentence: The lake freezed rapidly.
answers: The lake froze rapidly.
items.explanation: 'Freeze' is irregular: freeze – froze – frozen. 'Freezed' is not a word.

items.sentence: The firm was unwilling to forego its usual commission.
answers: The firm was unwilling to forgo its usual commission.
items.explanation: 'Forgo' means to do without; 'forego' strictly means to go before (as in 'a foregone conclusion'). Dictionaries now list 'forego' as a variant, but the exam expects 'forgo'.

items.sentence: We watched the lambs gamble on the green.
answers: We watched the lambs gambol on the green.
items.explanation: 'Gambol' means to skip and frisk about playfully; 'gamble' means to bet money.

items.sentence: He belonged to the gild of carpenters.
answers: He belonged to the guild of carpenters.
items.explanation: A 'guild' is an association of craftsmen; to 'gild' is to cover with gold.

items.sentence: He hadn't ought to have spoken.
answers: He ought not to have spoken.
He oughtn't to have spoken.
items.explanation: 'Ought' is a modal verb and forms its negative directly ('ought not'); it never takes 'had' as an auxiliary.

items.sentence: Hay! Watch out for the car!
answers: Hey! Watch out for the car!
items.explanation: The interjection used to call attention is 'Hey!'; 'hay' is dried grass.

items.sentence: This is the historical spot where he was shot dead.
answers: This is the historic spot where he was shot dead.
items.explanation: 'Historic' means famous or important in history; 'historical' simply means relating to history.

items.sentence: We bought a Japanee print.
answers: We bought a Japanese print.
items.explanation: The adjective from Japan is 'Japanese'.

items.sentence: Fresh flowers smell sweetly.
answers: Fresh flowers smell sweet.
items.explanation: 'Smell' here is a linking verb describing the subject, so it takes an adjective ('sweet'), not an adverb.

items.sentence: His wisdom consisted of his handling the dangerous situation successfully
answers: His wisdom consisted in his handling the dangerous situation successfully.
items.explanation: 'Consist of' means to be made up of; 'consist in' means to lie in or have as its essence, which is the sense here.

items.sentence: Many a girls were appearing in the examination.
answers: Many a girl was appearing in the examination.
Many girls were appearing in the examination.
items.explanation: 'Many a' is followed by a singular noun and a singular verb ('many a girl was'); otherwise use 'many girls were'.

items.sentence: The vehicles run fastly on the Motorway.
answers: The vehicles run fast on the Motorway.
items.explanation: 'Fast' is both adjective and adverb; 'fastly' does not exist.

items.sentence: Smoking is injurious for health.
answers: Smoking is injurious to health.
items.explanation: 'Injurious' takes the preposition 'to'.

items.sentence: He availed of this situation very intelligently.
answers: He availed himself of this situation very intelligently.
items.explanation: In the sense of 'make use of', 'avail' needs a reflexive pronoun: 'avail oneself of'.

items.sentence: The black vermin is an odious creature.
answers: The black vermin are odious creatures.
items.explanation: 'Vermin' is a plural noun, like 'cattle', so it takes a plural verb and cannot be 'a creature'.

items.sentence: What to speak of meat, even, vegetables were not available now.
answers: Not to speak of meat, even vegetables were not available now.
Not to speak of meat, even vegetables were not available then.
Even vegetables were not available now, let alone meat.
items.explanation: The idiom is 'not to speak of' (or 'let alone'); 'what to speak of' is a translation from Urdu. The comma after 'even' wrongly separates it from 'vegetables'.

items.sentence: No sooner we left our home when it started raining.
answers: No sooner had we left our home than it started raining.
items.explanation: 'No sooner' is followed by inversion with the past perfect ('had we left') and is paired with 'than', not 'when'.

items.sentence: Little money I had I spent on the way.
answers: The little money I had I spent on the way.
What little money I had I spent on the way.
items.explanation: 'Little' alone means 'hardly any'; 'the little' (or 'what little') means 'the small amount that I had', which is the sense here.

items.sentence: The criminal was sent on the goal.
answers: The criminal was sent to gaol.
The criminal was sent to jail.
items.explanation: The word is 'gaol' (British) or 'jail'; 'goal' is a target. One is sent 'to' gaol, with no article when the institution's purpose is meant.

items.sentence: I shall not come here unless you will not call me.
answers: I shall not come here unless you call me.
I shall not come here if you do not call me.
items.explanation: 'Unless' already means 'if not', so it cannot take another 'not'. A clause of condition also uses the present tense, not 'will'.

items.sentence: He does not have some devotion for the project you have given him.
answers: He does not have any devotion to the project you have given him.
He has no devotion to the project you have given him.
items.explanation: In negative sentences 'any' replaces 'some'. 'Devotion' takes the preposition 'to'.

items.sentence: I went to either of the Four hill stations.
answers: I went to one of the four hill stations.
items.explanation: 'Either' refers to one of two. With more than two, use 'one of' (or 'any of').

items.sentence: Who did you meet on your way to school?
answers: Whom did you meet on your way to school?
items.explanation: The pronoun is the object of 'meet', so strict grammar requires 'whom'. 'Who' is acceptable in everyday speech, but the exam expects the formal object form.

items.sentence: You must remember that you are junior than Hamid.
answers: You must remember that you are junior to Hamid.
items.explanation: Comparatives from Latin such as junior, senior, superior, inferior and prior take 'to', not 'than'.

items.sentence: Aslam, as well as, his Four friends were planning to visit the museum.
answers: Aslam, as well as his four friends, was planning to visit the museum.
items.explanation: A phrase introduced by 'as well as' does not change the subject; 'Aslam' is singular, so the verb is 'was'. The commas enclose the whole phrase 'as well as his four friends'.

items.sentence: Where you went in the vacation?
answers: Where did you go in the vacation?
Where did you go during the vacation?
items.explanation: A wh-question in the simple past needs the auxiliary 'did' before the subject, with the base form of the verb.

items.sentence: This is the youngest and most intelligent of my two sons.
answers: This is the younger and more intelligent of my two sons.
items.explanation: When only two are compared, use the comparative ('younger', 'more intelligent'), not the superlative.

items.sentence: I congratulate you for your success.
answers: I congratulate you on your success.
items.explanation: One congratulates someone 'on' an achievement.

items.sentence: The hostel provides boarding and lodging to students.
answers: The hostel provides board and lodging to students.
The hostel provides board and lodging for students.
items.explanation: The fixed expression is 'board and lodging' ('board' meaning meals).

items.sentence: My cousin-brother will come to meet me.
answers: My cousin will come to meet me.
items.explanation: 'Cousin-brother' is a South Asian expression; standard English simply says 'cousin'.

items.sentence: He lives backside of my house.
answers: He lives behind my house.
He lives at the back of my house.
items.explanation: 'Backside' means the buttocks; the correct expression is 'behind' or 'at the back of'.

items.sentence: You have read it. Isn't it?
answers: You have read it, haven't you?
items.explanation: A question tag repeats the auxiliary of the main clause ('have') with the opposite polarity and the subject pronoun: 'haven't you?'. 'Isn't it?' is not a universal tag.

items.sentence: We discussed about this question.
answers: We discussed this question.
items.explanation: 'Discuss' is transitive and takes a direct object; 'about' is not used after it.

items.sentence: I am studying in an University for an year.
answers: I have been studying at a university for a year.
I have been studying in a university for a year.
items.explanation: 'University' and 'year' begin with a consonant sound (/j/), so they take 'a'. An action continuing up to now over a period ('for a year') needs the present perfect continuous.

items.sentence: Neither he nor I are at fault.
answers: Neither he nor I am at fault.
items.explanation: With 'neither … nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'I', so it is 'am'.

items.sentence: The committee have issued a notice.
answers: The committee has issued a notice.
items.explanation: A collective noun acting as one body takes a singular verb. British English allows 'have' when members act individually, so the sentence is arguably acceptable, but issuing a notice is a single act, so the exam expects 'has'.

items.sentence: One must boast of his great qualities.
answers: One must not boast of one's great qualities.
One must boast of one's great qualities.
items.explanation: In formal English 'one' is followed by 'one's', not 'his'. The intended sense is almost certainly 'must not boast'.

items.sentence: Passing through ten different cities, Karachi is the most active.
answers: Passing through ten different cities, I found Karachi the most active.
Passing through ten different cities, I found Karachi to be the most active.
Of the ten different cities I passed through, Karachi is the most active.
items.explanation: The participle 'passing' must refer to the subject of the main clause; Karachi did not pass through the cities, so a proper subject (I) is needed.

items.sentence: Someone showed the visitors in the room.
answers: Someone showed the visitors into the room.
items.explanation: Movement from outside to inside takes 'into'; 'in' describes position.

items.sentence: Until you remain idle you will make no progress.
answers: As long as you remain idle, you will make no progress.
So long as you remain idle, you will make no progress.
If you remain idle, you will make no progress.
items.explanation: 'Until' means 'up to the time when' and makes no sense here; the meaning 'during the whole time that' needs 'as long as' (or 'so long as').

items.sentence: It is very wrong to be devoted to lying and cheating.
answers: It is very wrong to be addicted to lying and cheating.
It is very wrong to be given to lying and cheating.
items.explanation: 'Devoted to' is used for good things (one's duty, family); for bad habits use 'addicted to' or 'given to'.

items.sentence: He told me that he is waiting for me since a long time.
answers: He told me that he had been waiting for me for a long time.
items.explanation: After the past reporting verb 'told', the tense shifts back to the past perfect continuous. A period of time ('a long time') takes 'for', not 'since'.

items.sentence: The house stood up in the dull street because of its red door.
answers: The house stood out in the dull street because of its red door.
items.explanation: 'Stand out' means to be conspicuous; 'stand up' means to rise to one's feet.

items.sentence: He brought the articles to the market which he wanted to sell.
answers: He brought to the market the articles which he wanted to sell.
He brought the articles which he wanted to sell to the market.
items.explanation: A relative clause should come right after the noun it describes; here 'which he wanted to sell' seems to describe the market instead of the articles.

items.sentence: What does a patient tell a doctor it is confidential?
answers: What a patient tells a doctor is confidential.
items.explanation: The noun clause 'What a patient tells a doctor' is the subject of 'is'; it takes statement word order (no 'does'), and the extra subject 'it' must go.

items.sentence: Did they not consider this as quiet convincing
answers: Did they not consider this quite convincing?
items.explanation: 'Consider' takes its complement directly, without 'as'. 'Quiet' (silent) is confused with 'quite' (fairly), and a question needs a question mark.

items.sentence: St Peter's at Rome is the largest of all other churches
answers: St Peter's at Rome is the largest of all churches.
St Peter's at Rome is larger than all other churches.
items.explanation: A superlative includes the thing being compared, so 'other' cannot follow it; 'other' belongs with the comparative ('larger than all other churches').

items.sentence: They succeeded with hardly making any effort
answers: They succeeded with hardly any effort.
They succeeded with very little effort.
items.explanation: 'With' is followed here by a noun phrase ('hardly any effort'), not a gerund clause.

items.sentence: Whatever have you done!
answers: What ever have you done?
Whatever have you done?
items.explanation: This is a question, so it ends with a question mark. Strict usage writes the emphatic interrogative as two words, 'what ever'; 'whatever' is now common, so the sentence is arguably acceptable apart from the punctuation.

items.sentence: The officers were given places according to their respective ranks
answers: The officers were given places according to their ranks.
items.explanation: 'Their' already links each officer with his own rank, so 'respective' adds nothing. The sentence is arguably acceptable, but the exam treats 'respective' as redundant.

items.sentence: A good reader must be hardworking and possess intelligence.
answers: A good reader must be hardworking and intelligent.
items.explanation: Items joined by 'and' should have the same form: two adjectives ('hardworking and intelligent').

items.sentence: I noticed Akbar was carrying a bag in his hand.
answers: I noticed that Akbar was carrying a bag.
I noticed Akbar carrying a bag.
items.explanation: A bag is carried in the hand, so 'in his hand' is redundant. The sentence is grammatical and arguably acceptable, but the exam expects the redundant phrase to go.

items.sentence: Having entered his house, the door was shut at one.
answers: Having entered his house, he shut the door at once.
Having entered his house, he at once shut the door.
items.explanation: 'Having entered' must refer to the subject of the main clause; the door did not enter the house, so 'he' must be the subject. 'At one' should be 'at once'.

items.sentence: He thinks that his writing is better than his friend.
answers: He thinks that his writing is better than his friend's.
He thinks that his writing is better than that of his friend.
items.explanation: Like must be compared with like: his writing with his friend's writing, not with his friend.

items.sentence: He is such a man who is liked by everyone.
answers: He is such a man as is liked by everyone.
He is the kind of man who is liked by everyone.
He is a man who is liked by everyone.
items.explanation: 'Such' is followed by the relative 'as', not 'who'.

items.sentence: I sent a verbal message to my friend.
answers: I sent an oral message to my friend.
items.explanation: Strictly, 'verbal' means 'in words' (spoken or written) and 'oral' means 'spoken'. 'Verbal message' is common usage, so the sentence is arguably acceptable, but the exam expects 'oral'.

items.sentence: He has visited as many historical places as one has or can visit.
answers: He has visited as many historical places as one has visited or can visit.
He has visited as many historical places as anyone has visited or can visit.
items.explanation: A verb can be left out only if it matches both auxiliaries; 'has … visit' does not, so 'has visited' must be written in full.

items.sentence: Please tell me where is your brother?
answers: Please tell me where your brother is.
items.explanation: An indirect question uses statement word order ('where your brother is') and ends with a full stop.

items.sentence: Sajjad as well as Saleem were late.
answers: Sajjad, as well as Saleem, was late.
Sajjad as well as Saleem was late.
items.explanation: 'As well as Saleem' does not add to the subject; 'Sajjad' is singular, so the verb is 'was'.

items.sentence: He is the most cleverest boy in the class.
answers: He is the cleverest boy in the class.
items.explanation: 'Cleverest' is already superlative; adding 'most' makes a double superlative.

items.sentence: I have met him last month.
answers: I met him last month.
items.explanation: A finished past time ('last month') takes the simple past, not the present perfect.

items.sentence: Your writing is inferior than him.
answers: Your writing is inferior to his.
items.explanation: 'Inferior' takes 'to', not 'than', and writing must be compared with writing ('his'), not with a person ('him').

items.sentence: Nothing but novels please him.
answers: Nothing but novels pleases him.
items.explanation: The subject is 'nothing', which is singular; 'but novels' does not change it.

items.sentence: The teacher gave the boy an advice which he refused.
answers: The teacher gave the boy a piece of advice, which he refused.
The teacher gave the boy some advice, which he refused.
The teacher gave the boy advice, which he refused.
items.explanation: 'Advice' is uncountable, so it cannot take 'an'; use 'a piece of advice', 'some advice' or 'advice'.

items.sentence: He swore from God
answers: He swore by God.
items.explanation: One swears 'by' God (or by something sacred).

items.sentence: Is your dress different than mine?
answers: Is your dress different from mine?
Is your dress different to mine?
items.explanation: 'Different from' is the standard form ('different to' is also British). 'Different than' is common in American English, so it is arguably acceptable, but the exam expects 'from'.

items.sentence: He inquired whether I live in Karachi.
answers: He inquired whether I lived in Karachi.
He enquired whether I lived in Karachi.
items.explanation: After a past reporting verb, the present tense shifts back to the past: 'lived'.

items.sentence: He spoke these words upon his face.
answers: He spoke these words to his face.
items.explanation: To say something directly in someone's presence is to say it 'to his face'.

items.sentence: They ran direct to their college.
answers: They ran directly to their college.
They ran straight to their college.
items.explanation: 'Direct' can be an adverb ('go direct'), so the sentence is arguably acceptable, but the exam expects the regular adverb 'directly' (or 'straight').

items.sentence: They have been building a wall since three days.
answers: They have been building a wall for three days.
items.explanation: 'For' is used with a period of time (three days); 'since' with a point in time (Monday, 2009).

items.sentence: He does not have some devotion to his studies.
answers: He does not have any devotion to his studies.
He has no devotion to his studies.
items.explanation: In negative sentences 'some' becomes 'any' (or use 'no' with a positive verb).

items.sentence: This house is built of bricks and stones.
answers: This house is built of brick and stone.
items.explanation: Names of materials are uncountable when the substance is meant ('built of brick and stone'). The plural is arguably acceptable for individual bricks, but the exam expects the material form.

items.sentence: The climate of Pakistan is better than England?
answers: The climate of Pakistan is better than that of England.
items.explanation: Climate must be compared with climate ('that of England'), not with a country. The statement also ends with a full stop, not a question mark.

items.sentence: You ought to have regarded him your benefactor.
answers: You ought to have regarded him as your benefactor.
items.explanation: 'Regard' takes 'as' before its complement: 'regard someone as something'.

items.sentence: My friend is very ill, I hope he will soon die.
answers: My friend is very ill; I fear he will soon die.
My friend is very ill, and I fear he will soon die.
My friend is very ill. I fear he will soon die.
items.explanation: 'Hope' is used for something desired, 'fear' for something dreaded. Two main clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone.

items.sentence: He is waiting for better and promising opportunity.
answers: He is waiting for a better and more promising opportunity.
items.explanation: A singular countable noun needs an article ('a … opportunity'), and both adjectives must be comparative ('better and more promising').

items.sentence: When I shall see her I will deliver her your gift.
answers: When I see her, I will give her your gift.
When I see her, I will deliver your gift to her.
When I see her, I shall deliver your gift to her.
items.explanation: A time clause about the future uses the present tense ('when I see her'), not 'shall'. 'Deliver' takes 'to' before the receiver.

items.sentence: Many a sleepless nights she spent.
answers: Many a sleepless night she spent.
items.explanation: 'Many a' is always followed by a singular noun.

items.sentence: Please speak to the concerned clerk.
answers: Please speak to the clerk concerned.
items.explanation: In the sense 'involved or responsible', 'concerned' follows the noun; before the noun it means 'worried'.

items.sentence: You have got time too short for that.
answers: You have got too short a time for that.
You have too little time for that.
items.explanation: With 'too' and a singular noun, the order is 'too + adjective + a + noun': 'too short a time'.

items.sentence: Not only he was a thief, but he was also a murderer.
answers: Not only was he a thief, but he was also a murderer.
He was not only a thief but also a murderer.
items.explanation: When 'not only' begins a clause, the subject and verb are inverted: 'Not only was he …'.

items.sentence: They thought that the plan would be succeeded.
answers: They thought that the plan would succeed.
items.explanation: 'Succeed' is intransitive here and cannot be made passive.

items.sentence: It is unlikely that he wins the race.
answers: It is unlikely that he will win the race.
items.explanation: The race has not happened yet, so the future 'will win' is needed.

items.sentence: My uncle has told me something about it yesterday.
answers: My uncle told me something about it yesterday.
items.explanation: A finished past time ('yesterday') takes the simple past, not the present perfect.

items.sentence: I hoped that by the time I would have got there it would have stopped raining.
answers: I hoped that by the time I got there it would have stopped raining.
items.explanation: A time clause after 'by the time' takes the simple past here ('got'), not a conditional form; only the main clause uses 'would have'.

items.sentence: They prevented the driver to stop.
answers: They prevented the driver from stopping.
items.explanation: 'Prevent' is followed by an object + 'from' + gerund, not an infinitive.

items.sentence: A ten-feet long snake made people run here and there.
answers: A ten-foot-long snake made people run here and there.
A ten-foot long snake made people run here and there.
A snake ten feet long made people run here and there.
items.explanation: When a number + noun forms an adjective before a noun, the noun stays singular: 'a ten-foot-long snake' (but 'a snake ten feet long').

items.sentence: We are going to the concert, and so they are.
answers: We are going to the concert, and so are they.
items.explanation: 'So' meaning 'also' is followed by inversion: 'so are they'. 'So they are' means 'indeed they are'.

items.sentence: Enclosed with this letter was a signed Affidavit and a carbon copy of his request to our main office.
answers: Enclosed with this letter were a signed affidavit and a carbon copy of his request to our main office.
items.explanation: In an inverted sentence the subject follows the verb; here it is 'a signed affidavit and a carbon copy', which is plural, so the verb is 'were'. 'Affidavit' is a common noun and takes no capital.

items.sentence: Fear from God.
answers: Fear God.
items.explanation: 'Fear' takes a direct object; 'from' is not used after it.

items.sentence: Pakistan has and will support the Kashmiris.
answers: Pakistan has supported and will support the Kashmiris.
Pakistan has supported, and will support, the Kashmiris.
items.explanation: 'Has' needs the past participle 'supported'; the base form 'support' fits only 'will', so both verbs must be written in full.

items.sentence: He has come yesterday.
answers: He came yesterday.
items.explanation: A finished past time ('yesterday') takes the simple past, not the present perfect.

items.sentence: Arshad's down fall was due to nothing else than pride.
answers: Arshad's downfall was due to nothing other than pride.
Arshad's downfall was due to nothing else but pride.
Arshad's downfall was due to nothing but pride.
items.explanation: 'Else' is followed by 'but', and 'other' by 'than'; 'else than' is not idiomatic. 'Downfall' is one word.

items.sentence: Do not avoid to consult a doctor.
answers: Do not avoid consulting a doctor.
items.explanation: 'Avoid' is followed by a gerund ('consulting'), not an infinitive.

items.sentence: My boss agreed with my plan.
answers: My boss agreed to my plan.
items.explanation: One agrees 'with' a person or opinion but 'to' a plan or proposal (meaning accepts it). 'Agreed with my plan' is common, so it is arguably acceptable, but the exam expects 'to'.

items.sentence: If he was here, he would be as wise as he was during the war.
answers: If he were here, he would be as wise as he was during the war.
items.explanation: An unreal present condition takes the subjunctive 'were' for all persons. 'Was' is common in speech, but the exam expects 'were'.

items.sentence: We have amusements in form of music.
answers: We have amusements in the form of music.
items.explanation: The fixed phrase is 'in the form of'.

items.sentence: You get hungry for all the work you have to do.
answers: You get hungry from all the work you have to do.
You get hungry because of all the work you have to do.
You get hungry after all the work you have to do.
items.explanation: 'Hungry for' means 'eager for', which is not the sense; the cause of hunger is expressed with 'from' or 'because of'.

items.sentence: We were glad for being there.
answers: We were glad to be there.
items.explanation: 'Glad' is followed by an infinitive ('glad to be'), not 'for' + gerund.

items.sentence: I prefer the fifth act of Shakespeare King Lear the best of all.
answers: I like the fifth act of Shakespeare's King Lear best of all.
I like the fifth act of Shakespeare's King Lear the best of all.
I prefer the fifth act of Shakespeare's King Lear to all the others.
items.explanation: 'Prefer' already means 'like better', so it cannot take 'the best of all'; use 'like … best' or 'prefer … to'. The author's name needs the possessive: 'Shakespeare's'.

items.sentence: After finishing my lecture, the bell rang.
answers: After I had finished my lecture, the bell rang.
After I finished my lecture, the bell rang.
After finishing my lecture, I heard the bell ring.
items.explanation: The bell did not finish the lecture; the phrase needs a subject of its own ('I') or the main clause must have 'I' as its subject.

items.sentence: We needed not to be afraid.
answers: We need not have been afraid.
We did not need to be afraid.
items.explanation: As a main verb, 'need' forms its negative with 'did not' ('did not need to'); as a modal it is 'need not', with 'have been' for the past. 'Needed not to be' mixes the two.

items.sentence: Each furniture in this display is on sale for half price.
answers: Each piece of furniture in this display is on sale for half price.
items.explanation: 'Furniture' is uncountable, so it cannot follow 'each'; use 'each piece of furniture'.

items.sentence: He is abusing the money of his father.
answers: He is misusing his father's money.
He is misusing the money of his father.
He is squandering his father's money.
items.explanation: One 'misuses' or 'squanders' money; 'abuse' is used for people, power or trust. With a person, the possessive 's ('his father's money') is more natural than 'of his father'.

items.sentence: The duties of the new secretary are to answer the telephone, to type letters and bookkeeping.
answers: The duties of the new secretary are to answer the telephone, to type letters and to do the bookkeeping.
The duties of the new secretary are answering the telephone, typing letters and bookkeeping.
items.explanation: Items in a list must have the same form: all infinitives ('to answer … to type … to do the bookkeeping') or all gerunds.

items.sentence: The new models are not only less expensive but more efficient also.
answers: The new models are not only less expensive but also more efficient.
items.explanation: The pair is 'not only … but also', with 'also' placed right after 'but' and before the parallel element.

items.sentence: He complied with the requirement that all graduate students in education should write a thesis.
answers: He complied with the requirement that all graduate students in education write a thesis.
items.explanation: After nouns like 'requirement' the subjunctive base form is used ('that all students write'). British English also accepts 'should write', so the sentence is arguably acceptable; the exam expects the subjunctive.

items.sentence: No sooner we left the shop it began to rain.
answers: No sooner had we left the shop than it began to rain.
items.explanation: 'No sooner' is followed by inversion with the past perfect ('had we left') and paired with 'than'.

items.sentence: The population of Karachi is greater than any other city in Pakistan.
answers: The population of Karachi is greater than that of any other city in Pakistan.
items.explanation: Population must be compared with population ('that of any other city'), not with a city.

items.sentence: Have either of you seen my pen?
answers: Has either of you seen my pen?
items.explanation: 'Either' (one of the two) is singular, so it takes 'has'.

items.sentence: On attempting to restore the picture to its original condition, almost irreparable change was discovered.
answers: On attempting to restore the picture to its original condition, they discovered almost irreparable change.
When they attempted to restore the picture to its original condition, they discovered almost irreparable change.
items.explanation: 'On attempting' needs a subject that did the attempting; the passive 'change was discovered' leaves the phrase dangling, so the main clause must name the people (they).

items.sentence: The child is the prettiest of the two.
answers: The child is the prettier of the two.
items.explanation: When only two are compared, use the comparative ('the prettier').

items.sentence: I was annoyed arriving late, also his rather insolent manner put me out of temper.
answers: I was annoyed at arriving late, and his rather insolent manner also put me out of temper.
I was annoyed at arriving late; moreover, his rather insolent manner put me out of temper.
items.explanation: 'Annoyed' takes 'at' before a gerund. 'Also' is an adverb, not a conjunction, so it cannot join two clauses after a comma; use 'and … also' or a semicolon with 'moreover'.

items.sentence: He is anxious not only to acquire knowledge, but also eager to display it.
answers: He is not only anxious to acquire knowledge but also eager to display it.
items.explanation: 'Not only' and 'but also' must stand before parallel elements: 'not only anxious to acquire … but also eager to display'.

items.sentence: If he was here now, we should have no difficulty.
answers: If he were here now, we should have no difficulty.
If he were here now, we would have no difficulty.
items.explanation: An unreal present condition takes the subjunctive 'were'. 'Should' with 'we' is correct British usage; 'would' is also accepted.

items.sentence: Due to unforeseen environments, we shall have to leave early.
answers: Owing to unforeseen circumstances, we shall have to leave early.
Due to unforeseen circumstances, we shall have to leave early.
items.explanation: Situations are 'circumstances', not 'environments'. Strict usage prefers 'owing to' for an adverbial phrase of cause, keeping 'due to' after a noun or 'be'.

items.sentence: People have and still do disagree on this matter.
answers: People have disagreed and still do disagree on this matter.
People have disagreed, and still disagree, on this matter.
items.explanation: 'Have' needs the past participle 'disagreed'; it cannot borrow the base form 'disagree' from the 'do' clause.

items.sentence: We were staying at my sister's cape's code vacation home.
answers: We were staying at my sister's Cape Cod vacation home.
items.explanation: 'Cape Cod' is a proper noun: it takes capitals and is not possessive. Only 'sister's' needs the apostrophe.

items.sentence: She recommended me that I take a few days off from work.
answers: She recommended that I take a few days off from work.
She recommended that I should take a few days off from work.
items.explanation: 'Recommend' is followed directly by a 'that' clause; it does not take a personal object before it like 'tell'.

items.sentence: I tried to explain him the problem, but he had difficulty understanding me.
answers: I tried to explain the problem to him, but he had difficulty understanding me.
items.explanation: 'Explain' does not take two objects; the person comes after 'to': 'explain the problem to him'.

items.sentence: I'll do the grocery shopping for you grandma, Lucy said.
answers: "I'll do the grocery shopping for you, Grandma," Lucy said.
'I'll do the grocery shopping for you, Grandma,' Lucy said.
items.explanation: Spoken words go inside quotation marks, a comma separates the speech from 'Lucy said', and the name used in address ('Grandma') is set off by a comma and capitalised.

items.sentence: I don't know why you didn't go. If I were you, I should have gone.
answers: I don't know why you didn't go. If I had been you, I would have gone.
I don't know why you didn't go. If I had been you, I should have gone.
items.explanation: A condition about the past takes the past perfect ('If I had been you') with 'would/should have gone'.

items.sentence: Kevin says he stopped to travel internationally because of his family.
answers: Kevin says he stopped travelling internationally because of his family.
Kevin says he stopped traveling internationally because of his family.
items.explanation: 'Stop doing' means to give up an activity; 'stop to do' means to pause in order to do something. The sense here needs the gerund.

items.sentence: Don't run! Mr. Salman shouted.
answers: "Don't run!" Mr. Salman shouted.
'Don't run!' Mr Salman shouted.
Mr. Salman shouted, "Don't run!"
items.explanation: The exact words spoken must be enclosed in quotation marks.

items.sentence: In the accident one of my arms was broken and my legs bruised.
answers: In the accident one of my arms was broken and my legs were bruised.
items.focus: Ellipsis of verb with different number
items.explanation: A verb can be left out only if it is the same in both clauses; 'one of my arms was' cannot supply 'were' for 'my legs'.

items.sentence: The people who had been raising slogans against the government for many hours they wanted increase in their salaries.
answers: The people who had been raising slogans against the government for many hours wanted an increase in their salaries.
items.explanation: 'The people' is already the subject, so 'they' repeats it. 'Increase' here is a countable noun and needs 'an'.

items.sentence: You have been working very hard for the last two years. Isn't it?
answers: You have been working very hard for the last two years, haven't you?
items.explanation: The tag repeats the auxiliary ('have') in the negative with the subject pronoun: 'haven't you?'. 'Isn't it?' is not a universal tag.

items.sentence: John could hardly do no better than to have caught a bass of such dimensions.
answers: John could hardly have done better than to catch a bass of such dimensions.
John could hardly do better than to catch a bass of such dimensions.
John could have done no better than to catch a bass of such dimensions.
items.explanation: 'Hardly' is already negative, so it cannot be combined with 'no'. The perfect belongs on the modal ('could have done'), with a plain infinitive after 'than to'.

items.sentence: I who have no chance to meet him would rather go with you instead of sitting at home.
answers: I, who have no chance to meet him, would rather go with you than sit at home.
I, who have no chance of meeting him, would rather go with you than sit at home.
items.explanation: 'Would rather' is paired with 'than' + base verb ('than sit'), not 'instead of'. The non-defining clause about 'I' is set off by commas.

items.sentence: He not only comes there for swimming but also for coaching new swimmers.
answers: He comes there not only for swimming but also for coaching new swimmers.
He comes there not only to swim but also to coach new swimmers.
items.explanation: 'Not only' must stand before the same kind of element as 'but also'; both introduce 'for' phrases, so 'not only' goes after 'comes there'.

items.sentence: When he visited the fair last time, he bought no less than twenty school bags.
answers: When he visited the fair last time, he bought no fewer than twenty school bags.
items.explanation: 'Fewer' is used with countable nouns (bags), 'less' with uncountable ones. 'No less than' is common idiomatically, so the sentence is arguably acceptable, but the exam expects 'fewer'.

items.sentence: Ten cattles were grazing in the field.
answers: Ten cattle were grazing in the field.
Ten head of cattle were grazing in the field.
items.explanation: 'Cattle' is already plural and never takes -s.

items.sentence: They only work when they have no money.
answers: They work only when they have no money.
items.explanation: 'Only' should stand next to the part it limits, here 'when they have no money'. The sentence is common in speech and arguably acceptable, but the exam expects careful placement.

items.sentence: They left the hotel here they had been staying in a motor-car.
answers: They left in a motor-car the hotel where they had been staying.
In a motor-car they left the hotel where they had been staying.
They left the hotel where they had been staying, in a motor-car.
items.explanation: 'Here' must be the relative 'where'. 'In a motor-car' describes how they left, so it must not sit after 'staying', where it suggests they had been staying in the car.

items.sentence: I cannot by no means allow you to do so.
answers: I cannot by any means allow you to do so.
I can by no means allow you to do so.
items.explanation: 'Cannot' and 'by no means' are both negative; use one: 'cannot by any means' or 'can by no means'.

items.sentence: My friend said he never remembered having read a more enjoyable book.
answers: My friend said he did not remember ever having read a more enjoyable book.
My friend said he could not remember ever having read a more enjoyable book.
items.explanation: 'Never remembered' suggests a repeated failure to recall; the sense is a single statement, so it is 'did not (or could not) remember ever having read'.

items.sentence: Going up the hill, an old temple was seen.
answers: Going up the hill, we saw an old temple.
Going up the hill, I saw an old temple.
As we went up the hill, we saw an old temple.
items.explanation: The temple was not going up the hill; the participle needs the people who were climbing as the subject of the main clause.

items.sentence: One day the bird did not perform certain tricks which had thought it to his satisfaction.
answers: One day the bird did not perform to his satisfaction certain tricks which he had taught it.
One day the bird did not perform, to his satisfaction, certain tricks which he had taught it.
items.explanation: The verb is 'taught' (from 'teach'), not 'thought', and the relative clause needs its subject 'he'. 'To his satisfaction' belongs with 'perform'.

items.sentence: I was rather impressed by the manner of the orator than by his matter.
answers: I was impressed rather by the manner of the orator than by his matter.
I was more impressed by the manner of the orator than by his matter.
items.explanation: 'Rather' must stand before the first of the two compared elements ('rather by the manner … than by his matter').

items.sentence: What an awful weather!
answers: What awful weather!
items.explanation: 'Weather' is uncountable, so it does not take 'a/an' in exclamations: 'What awful weather!'.

items.sentence: He enjoyed during the holidays.
answers: He enjoyed himself during the holidays.
items.explanation: 'Enjoy' is transitive and needs an object; to mean 'have a good time' it takes a reflexive pronoun.

items.sentence: None of the boys had learnt their lesson.
answers: None of the boys had learnt his lesson.
None of the boys had learned his lesson.
items.explanation: Strict grammar treats 'none' as 'not one', so the pronoun is singular ('his'). 'Their' is common today and arguably acceptable, but the exam expects the singular.

items.sentence: I regret at the delay.
answers: I regret the delay.
items.explanation: 'Regret' takes a direct object; 'at' is not used after it.

items.sentence: I could not help but laugh.
answers: I could not help laughing.
I couldn't help laughing.
items.explanation: Traditional usage is 'cannot help doing'. 'Cannot help but' is widely used and arguably acceptable, but the exam expects the gerund.

items.sentence: I always have and always shall be your friend.
answers: I have always been and shall always be your friend.
I have always been, and always shall be, your friend.
items.explanation: 'Have' needs the past participle 'been'; it cannot borrow 'be' from 'shall be', so both verbs must be written in full.

items.sentence: I was out walking when I saw the new moon in the garden.
answers: When I was out walking in the garden, I saw the new moon.
I was out walking in the garden when I saw the new moon.
items.explanation: 'In the garden' describes where I was walking; placed after 'the new moon' it says the moon was in the garden.

items.sentence: He cried as if he was mad.
answers: He cried as if he were mad.
items.explanation: 'As if' introduces an unreal comparison, which takes the subjunctive 'were'. 'Was' is common in speech, but the exam expects 'were'.

items.sentence: I won him in the race.
answers: I beat him in the race.
I defeated him in the race.
I won the race against him.
items.explanation: One 'wins' a race or a prize but 'beats' or 'defeats' a person.

items.sentence: He said that I am playing chess.
answers: He said that he was playing chess.
He said that I was playing chess.
items.explanation: After the past reporting verb 'said', the present continuous shifts back to the past continuous ('was playing'), with the pronoun changed to suit the speaker.

items.sentence: Unless you do not try, you will never succeed.
answers: Unless you try, you will never succeed.
items.explanation: 'Unless' already means 'if not', so it cannot be followed by another 'not'.

items.sentence: He wrote with ink.
answers: He wrote in ink.
items.explanation: We write 'in ink' or 'in pencil' (the medium) but 'with a pen' (the instrument).

items.sentence: What country he belongs to?
answers: What country does he belong to?
Which country does he belong to?
To what country does he belong?
items.explanation: A direct question in the simple present needs 'does' before the subject, with the base form of the verb.

items.sentence: When he reaches to manhood, he will visit to England.
answers: When he reaches manhood, he will visit England.
items.explanation: 'Reach' and 'visit' are transitive and take a direct object; 'to' is not used after them.

items.sentence: The new session commences from February 1st, 2020.
answers: The new session commences on February 1st, 2020.
The new session commences on 1st February, 2020.
The new session commences on 1 February 2020.
items.explanation: A point in time such as a date takes 'on'; 'commence from' is not idiomatic.

items.sentence: Please send this letter on my address.
answers: Please send this letter to my address.
items.explanation: Movement towards a destination takes 'to'.

items.sentence: They were lieing in the sun.
answers: They were lying in the sun.
items.explanation: Verbs ending in -ie change -ie to -y before -ing: lie – lying, die – dying.

items.sentence: He will not come without he is asked.
answers: He will not come unless he is asked.
items.explanation: 'Without' is a preposition and cannot introduce a clause; the conjunction meaning 'if not' is 'unless'.

items.sentence: John as well as Harry bear witness to it.
answers: John, as well as Harry, bears witness to it.
John as well as Harry bears witness to it.
items.explanation: 'As well as Harry' does not add to the subject; 'John' is singular, so the verb is 'bears'.

items.sentence: The crew was now on board and they soon busied themselves in preparing to meet the coming storm.
answers: The crew were now on board and they soon busied themselves in preparing to meet the coming storm.
The crew were now on board, and they soon busied themselves in preparing to meet the coming storm.
items.explanation: The pronouns 'they' and 'themselves' treat the crew as individual members, so the verb must also be plural: 'the crew were'.

items.sentence: Is there a sport club near by?
answers: Is there a sports club nearby?
items.explanation: The compound is 'sports club' (the plural form is fixed), and 'nearby' is written as one word.

items.sentence: The coat is quite big.
answers: The coat is too big.
items.explanation: 'Quite big' is grammatical, so the sentence is arguably acceptable; but to say the coat does not fit, the exam expects 'too', meaning 'more than is suitable'.

items.sentence: It's only a short travel by train.
answers: It's only a short journey by train.
It's only a short trip by train.
items.explanation: 'Travel' is usually an uncountable noun for travelling in general; a single trip is a 'journey' or 'trip'.

items.sentence: I must walk two miles to school every morning when I was a child.
answers: I had to walk two miles to school every morning when I was a child.
items.explanation: 'Must' has no past form; past obligation is expressed with 'had to'.

items.sentence: After the storm, we had got to pick up some fallen branches.
answers: After the storm, we had to pick up some fallen branches.
items.explanation: Past obligation is 'had to'; 'had got to' is not used for the past.

items.sentence: Guitar is most popular instrument among teen age boys, but not girls.
answers: The guitar is the most popular instrument among teenage boys, but not among girls.
The guitar is the most popular instrument among teenage boys but not among girls.
items.explanation: An instrument in general takes 'the' ('the guitar'), and a superlative needs 'the'. 'Teenage' is one word, and 'not girls' should repeat the preposition: 'not among girls'.

items.sentence: You are not well and I wish you feel better soon.
answers: You are not well, and I hope you feel better soon.
You are not well, and I hope you will feel better soon.
items.explanation: 'Hope' is used for something that may well happen; 'wish' + clause is for unreal situations. A comma comes before 'and' joining two main clauses.

items.sentence: The grass not looking green now because it is not raining since last month.
answers: The grass is not looking green now because it has not rained since last month.
The grass is not looking green now because it has not been raining since last month.
items.explanation: The continuous form needs 'is'. An action continuing from a past point ('since last month') takes the present perfect.

items.sentence: The cold air made me shiver a little when I was waiting for him.
answers: The cold air made me shiver a little while I was waiting for him.
The cold air made me shiver a little as I was waiting for him.
items.explanation: For a background action lasting a period of time, 'while' (or 'as') is the natural conjunction. 'When' is arguably acceptable, but the exam expects 'while'.

items.sentence: I offered my seat to an older woman who just smiled me.
answers: I offered my seat to an older woman, who just smiled at me.
I offered my seat to an older woman who just smiled at me.
I offered my seat to an elderly woman, who just smiled at me.
items.explanation: 'Smile' is intransitive; the person smiled to takes 'at'.

items.sentence: She packed her bags, carried downstairs and put the back seat of her car.
answers: She packed her bags, carried them downstairs and put them in the back seat of her car.
She packed her bags, carried them downstairs, and put them in the back seat of her car.
items.explanation: 'Carry' and 'put' are transitive and need an object ('them'), and 'put' needs a place phrase: 'in the back seat'.

items.sentence: Yesterday the principal said that the results will be announced the following week.
answers: Yesterday the principal said that the results would be announced the following week.
items.explanation: After a past reporting verb, 'will' shifts to 'would'.

items.sentence: The Prime Minister has visited China last month.
answers: The Prime Minister visited China last month.
items.explanation: A definite past time expression ('last month') requires the past simple, not the present perfect.

items.sentence: He has been living in Islamabad since ten years.
answers: He has been living in Islamabad for ten years.
items.explanation: 'For' is used with a length of time; 'since' with a point in time.

items.sentence: By the time the rescue team arrived, the flood washed away the bridge.
answers: By the time the rescue team arrived, the flood had washed away the bridge.
items.explanation: 'By the time' + past signals an earlier completed action, which takes the past perfect.

items.sentence: I will call you as soon as I will reach Karachi.
answers: I will call you as soon as I reach Karachi.
items.explanation: In time clauses ('as soon as', 'when', 'before', 'after', 'until'), the present tense is used for future time, not 'will'.

items.sentence: I am knowing the answer to this question.
answers: I know the answer to this question.
items.explanation: 'Know' is a stative verb and is not used in the continuous form.

items.sentence: Did she wrote the letter to the commissioner herself?
answers: Did she write the letter to the commissioner herself?
items.explanation: After 'did', the main verb is in the base form; the past is already shown by the auxiliary.

items.sentence: The jury have given its verdict in the murder case.
answers: The jury has given its verdict in the murder case.
The jury have given their verdict in the murder case.
items.explanation: Verb and pronoun must agree: a collective noun takes a singular verb with 'its' (one body) or a plural verb with 'their' (individuals), not a mixture.

items.sentence: The news of his promotion were received with joy.
answers: The news of his promotion was received with joy.
items.explanation: 'News' is uncountable and takes a singular verb despite its -s ending.

items.sentence: Either the principal or the teachers is responsible for discipline.
answers: Either the principal or the teachers are responsible for discipline.
items.explanation: With 'either ... or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject ('teachers').

items.sentence: Every student and teacher were present in the hall.
answers: Every student and teacher was present in the hall.
items.explanation: Subjects joined by 'and' but preceded by 'every' take a singular verb.

items.sentence: The minister, along with his secretaries, were present at the ceremony.
answers: The minister, along with his secretaries, was present at the ceremony.
