items.focus: Agreement: as well as, along with
items.explanation: A phrase introduced by 'along with' does not change the number of the subject; the verb agrees with 'minister'.

items.sentence: A number of students was absent today because of the heavy rain.
answers: A number of students were absent today because of the heavy rain.
items.explanation: 'A number of' means 'many' and takes a plural verb.

items.sentence: One of the boys have broken the window.
answers: One of the boys has broken the window.
items.explanation: The subject is 'one', so the verb is singular.

items.sentence: If I was the Prime Minister, I would ban plastic bags.
answers: If I were the Prime Minister, I would ban plastic bags.
items.explanation: In formal English, an unreal present condition uses 'were' for all persons.

items.sentence: I wish I can speak French as fluently as my sister.
answers: I wish I could speak French as fluently as my sister.
items.explanation: 'Wish' about the present is followed by a past form; 'can' becomes 'could'.

items.sentence: It is high time the government takes notice of rising prices.
answers: It is high time the government took notice of rising prices.
items.explanation: 'It is high time' + subject is followed by the past simple, though the meaning is present.

items.sentence: No sooner did the bell ring when the students rushed out.
answers: No sooner did the bell ring than the students rushed out.
items.explanation: 'No sooner' is always paired with 'than', not 'when'.

items.sentence: Hardly had I reached home than it started raining.
answers: Hardly had I reached home when it started raining.
Hardly had I reached home before it started raining.
items.explanation: 'Hardly' is paired with 'when' or 'before', not 'than'.

items.sentence: The new hospital will inaugurate by the Chief Minister tomorrow.
answers: The new hospital will be inaugurated by the Chief Minister tomorrow.
items.explanation: The hospital receives the action, so the passive 'will be' + past participle is needed.

items.sentence: You must to submit your application before Friday.
answers: You must submit your application before Friday.
items.explanation: Modal verbs such as 'must' are followed by the bare infinitive, without 'to'.

items.sentence: He is a doctor at the Services Hospital, isn't it?
answers: He is a doctor at the Services Hospital, isn't he?
items.explanation: The tag repeats the subject as a pronoun: 'he', not 'it'.

items.sentence: He enjoys to play cricket with his friends on Sundays.
answers: He enjoys playing cricket with his friends on Sundays.
items.explanation: 'Enjoy' is followed by a gerund, not a to-infinitive.

items.sentence: Let him to go home early today because he is unwell.
answers: Let him go home early today because he is unwell.
items.explanation: 'Let' + object is followed by the bare infinitive, without 'to'.

items.sentence: The doctor suggested him to rest for a week.
answers: The doctor suggested that he rest for a week.
The doctor suggested that he should rest for a week.
items.explanation: 'Suggest' is not followed by object + to-infinitive; use a that-clause with the subjunctive or 'should'.

items.sentence: The murderer was hung at the central jail in 1985.
answers: The murderer was hanged at the central jail in 1985.
items.explanation: For execution the past form is 'hanged'; 'hung' is used for objects.

items.sentence: He has swam across the river twice this summer.
answers: He has swum across the river twice this summer.
items.explanation: The past participle of 'swim' is 'swum'; 'swam' is the past tense.

items.sentence: He said me that he was busy with the census work.
answers: He told me that he was busy with the census work.
He said to me that he was busy with the census work.
items.explanation: 'Say' does not take a personal object directly; use 'tell me' or 'say to me'.

items.sentence: I am used to get up early for the dawn prayer.
answers: I am used to getting up early for the dawn prayer.
items.explanation: In 'be used to' (accustomed to), 'to' is a preposition and is followed by a gerund.

items.sentence: I thought that the train has already left the station.
answers: I thought that the train had already left the station.
items.explanation: A past main verb ('thought') is followed by a past tense; an action earlier than it takes the past perfect.

items.sentence: I have finished my thesis two weeks ago.
answers: I finished my thesis two weeks ago.
items.explanation: 'Ago' marks a finished past time, so the past simple is used.

items.sentence: The road has been closed for last Monday.
answers: The road has been closed since last Monday.
items.explanation: 'Since' marks the starting point of a period; 'for' gives its length.

items.sentence: I recognised her at once because I met her before.
answers: I recognised her at once because I had met her before.
items.explanation: An action earlier than another past action takes the past perfect.

items.sentence: Please wait here until the officer will return.
answers: Please wait here until the officer returns.
items.explanation: 'Will' is not used in a time clause introduced by 'until'; use the present simple.

items.sentence: This land is belonging to my uncle and his three sons.
answers: This land belongs to my uncle and his three sons.
items.explanation: 'Belong' expresses a state and is not used in the continuous.

items.sentence: He does not knows the way to the station.
answers: He does not know the way to the station.
items.explanation: After 'does', the main verb takes the base form without -s.

items.sentence: The committee was divided in their opinions on the new tax.
answers: The committee were divided in their opinions on the new tax.
items.explanation: When the members of a collective noun act as individuals (here, disagreeing), the verb is plural.

items.sentence: Economics are my favourite subject, and I hope to teach it.
answers: Economics is my favourite subject, and I hope to teach it.
items.explanation: Names of subjects ending in -ics (economics, physics) take a singular verb.

items.sentence: Neither the manager nor his clerks has signed the register.
answers: Neither the manager nor his clerks have signed the register.
items.explanation: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the subject closer to it.

items.sentence: Each of the provinces have its own assembly.
answers: Each of the provinces has its own assembly.
items.explanation: 'Each of' + plural noun takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: The teacher as well as the students were happy with the result.
answers: The teacher as well as the students was happy with the result.
items.focus: Agreement: as well as, along with
items.explanation: With 'as well as', the verb agrees with the first subject.

items.sentence: The number of unemployed graduates are rising every year.
answers: The number of unemployed graduates is rising every year.
items.explanation: 'The number of' refers to a single figure and takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: He is one of the best student in the class.
answers: He is one of the best students in the class.
items.explanation: 'One of the' is followed by a plural noun.

items.sentence: If he would have worked hard, he would have passed.
answers: If he had worked hard, he would have passed.
items.explanation: In a third conditional, the if-clause takes the past perfect, not 'would have'.

items.sentence: I wish I was born in a more peaceful age.
answers: I wish I had been born in a more peaceful age.
items.explanation: A wish about the past takes the past perfect.

items.sentence: It is time you start preparing for the CSS examination.
answers: It is time you started preparing for the CSS examination.
It is time for you to start preparing for the CSS examination.
items.explanation: 'It is time' takes a subject + past simple, or 'for' + object + to-infinitive.

items.sentence: No sooner he had entered the room than the lights went out.
answers: No sooner had he entered the room than the lights went out.
items.explanation: A sentence beginning with 'no sooner' requires inversion of subject and auxiliary.

items.sentence: Scarcely had the train left than the bomb exploded.
answers: Scarcely had the train left when the bomb exploded.
Scarcely had the train left before the bomb exploded.
items.explanation: 'Scarcely' takes 'when' or 'before'; 'than' belongs with 'no sooner'.

items.sentence: English is speaking in many countries of the world.
answers: English is spoken in many countries of the world.
items.explanation: The subject receives the action, so the passive form 'is spoken' is required.

items.sentence: He can speaks four languages, including Pashto and Balochi.
answers: He can speak four languages, including Pashto and Balochi.
items.explanation: A modal is followed by the base form of the verb, never the -s form.

items.sentence: You have finished the quarterly report, didn't you?
answers: You have finished the quarterly report, haven't you?
items.explanation: The tag uses the same auxiliary as the main clause ('have').

items.sentence: She managed passing the test on her second attempt.
answers: She managed to pass the test on her second attempt.
items.explanation: 'Manage' is followed by a to-infinitive.

items.sentence: Poverty made him to leave school early to support his family.
answers: Poverty made him leave school early to support his family.
items.explanation: In the active voice, 'make' + object takes the bare infinitive.

items.sentence: The opposition insisted to hold a fresh election.
answers: The opposition insisted on holding a fresh election.
items.explanation: 'Insist' takes 'on' + gerund, not a to-infinitive.

items.sentence: I was so tired that I laid down on the sofa.
answers: I was so tired that I lay down on the sofa.
items.explanation: 'Lie' (recline) has the past tense 'lay'; 'laid' is the past of 'lay' (put down).

items.sentence: The school bell has already rang, so hurry to class.
answers: The school bell has already rung, so hurry to class.
items.explanation: The past participle of 'ring' is 'rung'.

items.sentence: She asked me where was the post office.
answers: She asked me where the post office was.
items.explanation: Reported questions use statement word order (subject before verb).

items.sentence: He use to walk to school every day.
answers: He used to walk to school every day.
items.explanation: The past habit form is 'used to' in affirmative sentences.

items.sentence: She realised that she has left her purse in the rickshaw.
answers: She realised that she had left her purse in the rickshaw.
items.explanation: The leaving happened before the past realisation, so the past perfect is required.

items.sentence: When have you joined the civil service as an assistant commissioner?
answers: When did you join the civil service as an assistant commissioner?
items.explanation: Questions with 'when' ask about a point in past time and take the past simple.

items.sentence: I am waiting for the bus since seven o'clock.
answers: I have been waiting for the bus since seven o'clock.
items.explanation: An action that began in the past and continues now, with 'since', takes the present perfect continuous, not the present continuous.

items.sentence: He told the court that he never saw the accused before that day.
answers: He told the court that he had never seen the accused before that day.
items.explanation: Experience up to a past point ('before that day') takes the past perfect.

items.sentence: Before you will leave the office, switch off the lights.
answers: Before you leave the office, switch off the lights.
items.explanation: A clause beginning with 'before' takes the present tense for future reference.

items.sentence: She is having two brothers in the army.
answers: She has two brothers in the army.
items.explanation: 'Have' meaning possession is stative and is not used in the continuous.

items.sentence: Does your father works in a bank or in a government office?
answers: Does your father work in a bank or in a government office?
items.explanation: In questions with 'does', the main verb is in the base form.

items.sentence: The cattle is grazing in the field near the canal.
answers: The cattle are grazing in the field near the canal.
items.explanation: 'Cattle' is a plural noun and always takes a plural verb.

items.sentence: The machinery in this mill are very old.
answers: The machinery in this mill is very old.
items.explanation: 'Machinery' is an uncountable noun and takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: Either you or he are to blame for the delay.
answers: Either you or he is to blame for the delay.
items.explanation: The verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'he', which is singular.

items.sentence: Every one of the applicants were interviewed by the panel.
answers: Every one of the applicants was interviewed by the panel.
items.explanation: 'Every one of' is singular and takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: The captain, together with his players, are leaving for England tomorrow.
answers: The captain, together with his players, is leaving for England tomorrow.
items.focus: Agreement: as well as, along with
items.explanation: 'Together with' adds information but does not make the subject plural.

items.sentence: A large number of pilgrims has arrived in Makkah.
answers: A large number of pilgrims have arrived in Makkah.
items.explanation: 'A (large) number of' + plural noun takes a plural verb.

items.sentence: One of the ministers were absent from the cabinet meeting.
answers: One of the ministers was absent from the cabinet meeting.
items.explanation: The verb agrees with 'one', not with 'ministers'.

items.sentence: If I had known about the strike, I would not come to the office.
answers: If I had known about the strike, I would not have come to the office.
items.explanation: A past perfect if-clause pairs with 'would have' + past participle in the main clause.

items.sentence: She wishes she has more time to read.
answers: She wishes she had more time to read.
items.explanation: A wish about the present is expressed with the past simple.

items.sentence: It is high time we should end corruption.
answers: It is high time we ended corruption.
items.explanation: 'It is high time' is followed by the past simple, not by 'should'.

items.sentence: No sooner had the results been announced then the celebrations began.
answers: No sooner had the results been announced than the celebrations began.
items.explanation: The correlative is 'than', not 'then'.

items.sentence: Hardly he had finished his lunch when the phone rang.
answers: Hardly had he finished his lunch when the phone rang.
items.explanation: A sentence beginning with 'hardly' requires inversion of subject and auxiliary.

items.sentence: The bridge was build by the British in 1890.
answers: The bridge was built by the British in 1890.
items.explanation: The passive is formed with 'be' + past participle ('built').

items.sentence: She could not came to the wedding because of her examinations.
answers: She could not come to the wedding because of her examinations.
items.explanation: After a modal, the verb is in the base form.

items.sentence: Let's go for a walk along the canal, don't we?
answers: Let's go for a walk along the canal, shall we?
items.explanation: A suggestion with 'Let's' takes the tag 'shall we?'.

items.sentence: They decided postponing the elections until the floods had receded.
answers: They decided to postpone the elections until the floods had receded.
items.explanation: 'Decide' takes a to-infinitive.

items.sentence: I saw him to enter the building just before the explosion.
answers: I saw him enter the building just before the explosion.
I saw him entering the building just before the explosion.
items.explanation: Verbs of perception ('see', 'hear', 'feel') + object take the bare infinitive or the -ing form.

items.sentence: The committee recommended that the officer is suspended.
answers: The committee recommended that the officer be suspended.
The committee recommended that the officer should be suspended.
items.explanation: After 'recommend that', formal English uses the subjunctive or 'should'.

items.sentence: Please lie the files on my desk before you go home.
answers: Please lay the files on my desk before you go home.
items.explanation: 'Lay' (transitive) means 'put down' and takes an object; 'lie' does not.

items.sentence: He fell the old tree with an axe.
answers: He felled the old tree with an axe.
items.explanation: 'Fell' (cut down) is a regular transitive verb with the past 'felled'; 'fell' is also the past of intransitive 'fall'.

items.sentence: The teacher said that he is satisfied with our work.
answers: The teacher said that he was satisfied with our work.
items.explanation: After a past reporting verb, the present tense shifts to the past.

items.sentence: Did you used to live in Peshawar before your father was transferred?
answers: Did you use to live in Peshawar before your father was transferred?
items.explanation: After 'did', the base form 'use to' is required.

items.sentence: The officer worked late so that he can finish the audit before the deadline.
answers: The officer worked late so that he could finish the audit before the deadline.
items.explanation: In a purpose clause after a past main verb, 'can' becomes 'could'.

items.sentence: Pakistan has won the Cricket World Cup in 1992.
answers: Pakistan won the Cricket World Cup in 1992.
items.explanation: A stated past year ('in 1992') requires the past simple.

items.sentence: She is working at the bank for five years.
answers: She has been working at the bank for five years.
She has worked at the bank for five years.
items.explanation: A situation lasting up to now with 'for' + period takes the present perfect (continuous).

items.sentence: Until that day, I never travelled by air.
answers: Until that day, I had never travelled by air.
items.explanation: Experience up to a point in the past is expressed with the past perfect.

items.sentence: The bill will become law after the President will sign it.
answers: The bill will become law after the President signs it.
The bill will become law after the President has signed it.
items.explanation: In a time clause with 'after', use the present simple or present perfect, not 'will'.

items.sentence: We are understanding the problem much better now.
answers: We understand the problem much better now.
items.explanation: 'Understand' is a verb of mental state and takes simple tenses.

items.sentence: They did not attended the seminar on climate change.
answers: They did not attend the seminar on climate change.
items.explanation: 'Did not' is followed by the base form of the verb.

items.sentence: The people of Thar is suffering from a severe drought.
answers: The people of Thar are suffering from a severe drought.
items.explanation: 'People' meaning persons is plural and takes a plural verb.

items.sentence: His luggage were lost at the airport during his journey to London.
answers: His luggage was lost at the airport during his journey to London.
items.explanation: 'Luggage' is uncountable and takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: Neither he nor I are going to the wedding.
answers: Neither he nor I am going to the wedding.
items.explanation: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees in person and number with the nearer subject, 'I'.

items.sentence: Each boy and each girl have been given a laptop.
answers: Each boy and each girl has been given a laptop.
items.explanation: When 'each' precedes subjects joined by 'and', the verb is singular.

items.sentence: The principal, accompanied by his staff, were at the gate to receive us.
answers: The principal, accompanied by his staff, was at the gate to receive us.
items.focus: Agreement: as well as, along with
items.explanation: The verb agrees with the real subject, 'principal', not the noun in the parenthetical phrase.

items.sentence: The number of applicants for the post were very high.
answers: The number of applicants for the post was very high.
items.explanation: The subject is 'the number', which is singular.

items.sentence: One of the most important reason for poverty is illiteracy.
answers: One of the most important reasons for poverty is illiteracy.
items.explanation: 'One of the' + superlative takes a plural noun.

items.sentence: If she studies regularly, she would pass easily.
answers: If she studies regularly, she will pass easily.
If she studied regularly, she would pass easily.
items.explanation: A present-tense if-clause takes 'will'; a past-tense if-clause takes 'would'.

items.sentence: I wish I attended the conference last week.
answers: I wish I had attended the conference last week.
items.explanation: A regret about the past takes 'wish' + past perfect.

items.sentence: It is high time that the students are taught civic sense.
answers: It is high time that the students were taught civic sense.
items.explanation: After 'it is high time', the verb is in the past form, including in the passive.

items.sentence: No sooner the rain stopped than the children ran outside.
answers: No sooner had the rain stopped than the children ran outside.
No sooner did the rain stop than the children ran outside.
items.explanation: 'No sooner' at the start needs inverted word order with 'had' or 'did'.

items.sentence: Scarcely I had closed my eyes when the alarm went off.
answers: Scarcely had I closed my eyes when the alarm went off.
items.explanation: Negative adverbs such as 'scarcely' at the start of a sentence require inversion.

items.sentence: The accident was happened near the toll plaza.
answers: The accident happened near the toll plaza.
items.explanation: 'Happen' is intransitive and cannot be used in the passive.

items.sentence: You need not to worry about the fee.
answers: You need not worry about the fee.
You do not need to worry about the fee.
items.explanation: Modal 'need not' takes the bare infinitive; the main verb 'need' takes 'to'.

items.sentence: Nobody called while I was out, didn't they?
answers: Nobody called while I was out, did they?
items.explanation: 'Nobody' makes the statement negative, so the tag is positive.

items.sentence: Would you mind to close the door while I am on the phone?
answers: Would you mind closing the door while I am on the phone?
items.explanation: 'Mind' is followed by a gerund.

items.sentence: We heard the minister to say that taxes would rise.
answers: We heard the minister say that taxes would rise.
items.explanation: 'Hear' + object is followed by the bare infinitive in the active voice.

items.sentence: She suggested to go to Naran for the holidays.
answers: She suggested going to Naran for the holidays.
items.explanation: 'Suggest' is followed by a gerund or a that-clause, never a to-infinitive.

items.sentence: The sun raises in the east and sets in the west.
answers: The sun rises in the east and sets in the west.
items.explanation: 'Rise' is intransitive; 'raise' needs an object.

items.sentence: She has began a new job at the ministry.
answers: She has begun a new job at the ministry.
items.explanation: The past participle of 'begin' is 'begun'.

items.sentence: He told that he would come the next day.
answers: He said that he would come the next day.
items.explanation: 'Tell' needs a personal object; without one, use 'say'.

items.sentence: She is used to work under pressure in the newsroom.
answers: She is used to working under pressure in the newsroom.
items.explanation: 'Be used to' is followed by a gerund or noun.

items.sentence: The farmers hoped that the rain will come before the harvest.
answers: The farmers hoped that the rain would come before the harvest.
items.explanation: A past main verb ('hoped') is followed by 'would', not 'will', for a future seen from the past.

items.sentence: The State Bank has raised the policy rate yesterday.
answers: The State Bank raised the policy rate yesterday.
items.explanation: 'Yesterday' is a finished time, so the present perfect cannot be used.

items.sentence: They have not met each other since a long time.
answers: They have not met each other for a long time.
items.explanation: 'A long time' is a duration, so it takes 'for', not 'since'.

items.sentence: The guests left by the time we got to the reception.
answers: The guests had left by the time we got to the reception.
items.explanation: The earlier of two past actions, with 'by the time', takes the past perfect.

items.sentence: We shall start the meeting when everyone will arrive.
answers: We shall start the meeting when everyone arrives.
We shall start the meeting when everyone has arrived.
items.explanation: A 'when' clause about the future takes the present (or present perfect), not 'will'.

items.sentence: He is seeming tired after the long journey.
answers: He seems tired after the long journey.
items.explanation: 'Seem' is a linking stative verb and is not used in the continuous.

items.sentence: She doesn't likes spicy food even though she grew up in Hyderabad.
answers: She doesn't like spicy food even though she grew up in Hyderabad.
items.explanation: After 'doesn't', the verb takes the base form.

items.sentence: The majority of the voters has rejected the proposal.
answers: The majority of the voters have rejected the proposal.
items.explanation: 'The majority of' + plural noun refers to individuals and takes a plural verb.

items.sentence: The scenery of the northern areas are breathtaking.
answers: The scenery of the northern areas is breathtaking.
items.explanation: 'Scenery' is uncountable; the verb agrees with it, not with 'areas'.

items.sentence: Neither of the two candidates were qualified for the post.
answers: Neither of the two candidates was qualified for the post.
items.explanation: 'Neither of' means 'not one of the two' and takes a singular verb in formal English.

items.sentence: Everyone in the village know the old schoolmaster.
answers: Everyone in the village knows the old schoolmaster.
items.explanation: 'Everyone' is singular and takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: My brother, like my sisters, want to become a doctor.
answers: My brother, like my sisters, wants to become a doctor.
items.focus: Agreement: as well as, along with
items.explanation: A phrase beginning with 'like' does not affect the number of the subject.

items.sentence: A number of complaints has been received against the contractor.
answers: A number of complaints have been received against the contractor.
items.explanation: 'A number of' means 'several' and takes a plural verb.

items.sentence: One of my uncles live in Saudi Arabia.
answers: One of my uncles lives in Saudi Arabia.
items.explanation: The head of the subject is 'one', which takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: Had I knew the truth, I would have told you.
answers: Had I known the truth, I would have told you.
items.explanation: Inverted third conditionals use 'had' + past participle.

items.sentence: If only he listens to his parents and teachers!
answers: If only he would listen to his parents and teachers!
If only he listened to his parents and teachers!
items.explanation: 'If only', like 'wish', takes a past form or 'would' for present situations.

items.sentence: It is late, and it's high time you go to bed.
answers: It is late, and it's high time you went to bed.
items.explanation: 'It's high time' + subject requires the past simple.

items.sentence: No sooner had we sat down for dinner but the guests arrived.
answers: No sooner had we sat down for dinner than the guests arrived.
items.explanation: 'No sooner' takes 'than', not 'but'.

items.sentence: Barely had the plane taken off than the pilot reported a fault.
answers: Barely had the plane taken off when the pilot reported a fault.
items.explanation: 'Barely', like 'hardly' and 'scarcely', is followed by 'when', not 'than'.

items.sentence: The letter has been wrote by the director himself.
answers: The letter has been written by the director himself.
items.explanation: The passive needs the past participle 'written', not the past tense 'wrote'.

items.sentence: We ought respect our elders and look after them in old age.
answers: We ought to respect our elders and look after them in old age.
items.explanation: 'Ought' is always followed by 'to'.

items.sentence: She never misses a lecture on economics, doesn't she?
answers: She never misses a lecture on economics, does she?
items.explanation: 'Never' makes the sentence negative, so the tag must be positive.

items.sentence: He finished to write his thesis in May.
answers: He finished writing his thesis in May.
items.explanation: 'Finish' takes a gerund.

items.sentence: She helped me finding the right book in the library.
answers: She helped me find the right book in the library.
She helped me to find the right book in the library.
items.explanation: 'Help' + object takes the bare infinitive or the to-infinitive, not a gerund.

items.sentence: He insisted me to stay for dinner at his house.
answers: He insisted that I stay for dinner at his house.
He insisted that I should stay for dinner at his house.
He insisted on my staying for dinner at his house.
items.explanation: 'Insist' does not take object + to-infinitive; use a that-clause or 'insist on' + gerund.

items.sentence: The government has rose the price of petrol.
answers: The government has raised the price of petrol.
items.explanation: 'Raise' (transitive) is needed with an object; its past participle is 'raised'.

items.sentence: The guests have went home after the dinner.
answers: The guests have gone home after the dinner.
items.explanation: The past participle of 'go' is 'gone'.

items.sentence: Last week she said that she will meet me the next day.
answers: Last week she said that she would meet me the next day.
items.explanation: In indirect speech after a past reporting verb, 'will' becomes 'would'.

items.sentence: I used to playing hockey in college but now I prefer cricket.
answers: I used to play hockey in college but now I prefer cricket.
items.explanation: 'Used to' for past habit is followed by the base form of the verb.

items.sentence: We were told that the flight is delayed by three hours.
answers: We were told that the flight was delayed by three hours.
We were told that the flight had been delayed by three hours.
items.explanation: After a past main verb the subordinate verb moves into the past.

items.sentence: I did not see him since he moved to Quetta.
answers: I have not seen him since he moved to Quetta.
items.explanation: A period running from a past point up to now ('since ...') takes the present perfect in the main clause.

items.sentence: The country has faced load-shedding since many years.
answers: The country has faced load-shedding for many years.
items.explanation: 'Many years' is a period of time and takes 'for'.

items.sentence: I had visited Murree last summer with my family.
answers: I visited Murree last summer with my family.
items.explanation: The past perfect needs a later past reference point; a single past event at a stated time takes the past simple.

items.sentence: Once the dam will be completed, the region will get cheap electricity.
answers: Once the dam is completed, the region will get cheap electricity.
Once the dam has been completed, the region will get cheap electricity.
items.explanation: Time clauses with 'once' use the present tense for future meaning.

items.sentence: The soup is tasting delicious after a long day of fasting.
answers: The soup tastes delicious after a long day of fasting.
items.explanation: 'Taste' as a linking verb describing a quality is stative and takes the simple form.

items.sentence: Why did the minister resigned so suddenly last week?
answers: Why did the minister resign so suddenly last week?
items.explanation: The auxiliary 'did' carries the past tense; the main verb stays in the base form.

items.sentence: A bouquet of roses were presented to the chief guest.
answers: A bouquet of roses was presented to the chief guest.
items.explanation: The subject is the singular 'bouquet', not 'roses', so the verb is singular.

items.sentence: The information you gave us were incorrect and misleading.
answers: The information you gave us was incorrect and misleading.
items.explanation: 'Information' is uncountable and takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: Either of these roads lead to Abbottabad, so take whichever is shorter.
answers: Either of these roads leads to Abbottabad, so take whichever is shorter.
items.explanation: 'Either of' refers to one of two and takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: Each of these questions carry ten marks in the final examination.
answers: Each of these questions carries ten marks in the final examination.
items.explanation: 'Each of' takes a singular verb regardless of the plural noun after 'of'.

items.sentence: The house with all its furniture were sold last week.
answers: The house with all its furniture was sold last week.
items.focus: Agreement: as well as, along with
items.explanation: A subject followed by 'with' + noun remains singular.

items.sentence: The number of schools in the district have doubled.
answers: The number of schools in the district has doubled.
items.explanation: 'The number of' takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: One of the bridges on the motorway have collapsed.
answers: One of the bridges on the motorway has collapsed.
items.explanation: 'One of' + plural noun takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: If the government will reduce taxes, businesses will grow.
answers: If the government reduces taxes, businesses will grow.
items.explanation: In a first conditional, the if-clause takes the present tense, not 'will'.

items.sentence: He wishes he will become a pilot one day.
answers: He hopes he will become a pilot one day.
He wishes he could become a pilot one day.
items.explanation: 'Wish' is not followed by 'will'; use 'hope' for a possible future, or 'wish' + 'could'.

items.sentence: It is high time the assembly passes the bill.
answers: It is high time the assembly passed the bill.
items.explanation: The clause after 'it is high time' takes the past simple.

items.sentence: No sooner did the minister finished his speech than the crowd cheered.
answers: No sooner did the minister finish his speech than the crowd cheered.
items.explanation: After 'did', the main verb takes the base form.

items.sentence: Hardly had the meeting started then the power failed.
answers: Hardly had the meeting started when the power failed.
Hardly had the meeting started before the power failed.
items.explanation: The correct correlative for 'hardly' is 'when' or 'before', not 'then'.

items.sentence: My watch has stolen from the locker at the gym.
answers: My watch has been stolen from the locker at the gym.
items.explanation: The watch did not steal; it was stolen, so the present perfect passive 'has been stolen' is needed.

items.sentence: You had better to consult a doctor before the pain gets worse.
answers: You had better consult a doctor before the pain gets worse.
items.explanation: 'Had better' is followed by the bare infinitive.

items.sentence: I am right about the date of the meeting, amn't I?
answers: I am right about the date of the meeting, aren't I?
items.explanation: The negative tag for 'I am' is 'aren't I?' in standard English.

items.sentence: The minister refused answering the reporters' questions about the budget.
answers: The minister refused to answer the reporters' questions about the budget.
items.explanation: 'Refuse' is followed by a to-infinitive.

items.sentence: He was made apologise in public for his remarks.
answers: He was made to apologise in public for his remarks.
items.explanation: In the passive, 'make' is followed by the to-infinitive.

items.sentence: The minister recommended to increase the education budget.
answers: The minister recommended increasing the education budget.
The minister recommended that the education budget be increased.
items.explanation: 'Recommend' takes a gerund or a that-clause, not a to-infinitive.

items.sentence: The portraits were hanged on the walls of the museum.
answers: The portraits were hung on the walls of the museum.
items.explanation: For pictures and objects the past participle of 'hang' is 'hung'.

items.sentence: The overloaded boat has sank in the river.
answers: The overloaded boat has sunk in the river.
items.explanation: The past participle of 'sink' is 'sunk'.

items.sentence: He asked me that whether I had seen his book.
answers: He asked me whether I had seen his book.
items.explanation: A reported yes/no question is introduced by 'whether' or 'if', not 'that whether'.

items.sentence: We didn't used to have electricity in our village.
answers: We didn't use to have electricity in our village.
items.explanation: In negatives with 'didn't', the form is 'use to'.

items.sentence: He did not know where his son has gone.
answers: He did not know where his son had gone.
items.explanation: An action completed before a past moment takes the past perfect, not the present perfect.

items.sentence: Did you ever visit the Badshahi Mosque in Lahore?
answers: Have you ever visited the Badshahi Mosque in Lahore?
items.explanation: In British English, 'ever' asking about experience up to now takes the present perfect.

items.sentence: It is three years since he has left the village.
answers: It is three years since he left the village.
items.explanation: In 'It is + period + since ...', the since-clause takes the past simple.

items.sentence: By 1947 the Muslim League won the support of most Muslims in India.
answers: By 1947 the Muslim League had won the support of most Muslims in India.
items.explanation: 'By' + a past time shows completion before that point and takes the past perfect.

items.sentence: I will not rest till the work will be done.
answers: I will not rest till the work is done.
items.explanation: A clause introduced by 'till' takes the present tense, not 'will', for future time.

items.sentence: I am not believing a word of his story.
answers: I do not believe a word of his story.
I don't believe a word of his story.
items.explanation: 'Believe' is a stative verb of opinion and is not used in the continuous.

items.sentence: He didn't took any leave last year despite his illness.
answers: He didn't take any leave last year despite his illness.
items.explanation: 'Didn't' must be followed by the base form, not the past tense.

items.sentence: The government have announced its new trade policy.
answers: The government has announced its new trade policy.
The government have announced their new trade policy.
items.explanation: A collective noun must be treated consistently: singular verb with 'its' or plural verb with 'their'.

items.sentence: Physics have always been a difficult subject for me.
answers: Physics has always been a difficult subject for me.
items.explanation: 'Physics' as a subject is singular.

items.sentence: Neither the rain nor the cold weather have stopped the marchers.
answers: Neither the rain nor the cold weather has stopped the marchers.
items.explanation: Two singular subjects joined by 'neither ... nor' take a singular verb.

items.sentence: Every citizen have the right to vote in the general election.
answers: Every citizen has the right to vote in the general election.
items.explanation: 'Every' + singular noun takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: The farmer, as well as his sons, work in the fields from dawn.
answers: The farmer, as well as his sons, works in the fields from dawn.
items.focus: Agreement: as well as, along with
items.explanation: With 'as well as', the verb agrees with the first subject, 'farmer'.

items.sentence: A number of factories was closed due to the gas shortage.
answers: A number of factories were closed due to the gas shortage.
items.explanation: 'A number of' + plural noun takes a plural verb.

items.sentence: Lahore is one of the oldest city in the subcontinent.
answers: Lahore is one of the oldest cities in the subcontinent.
items.explanation: After 'one of the', the noun must be plural.

items.sentence: If I were you, I will apply for the post immediately.
answers: If I were you, I would apply for the post immediately.
items.explanation: An unreal condition with 'were' is followed by 'would' in the main clause.

items.sentence: We wish the government took action last year.
answers: We wish the government had taken action last year.
items.explanation: A wish about a past situation requires the past perfect.

items.sentence: It is high time we have a national language policy.
answers: It is high time we had a national language policy.
items.explanation: 'It is high time' is followed by a past-tense verb.

items.sentence: No sooner had he reach the station than the train left.
answers: No sooner had he reached the station than the train left.
items.explanation: 'Had' must be followed by the past participle.

items.sentence: Hardly did the teacher entered the class when the students stood up.
answers: Hardly did the teacher enter the class when the students stood up.
Hardly had the teacher entered the class when the students stood up.
items.explanation: After inverted 'did', the main verb takes the base form.

items.sentence: The results were declare on the board's website last Friday.
answers: The results were declared on the board's website last Friday.
items.explanation: A passive verb requires the past participle after 'be'.

items.sentence: I would rather to stay at home tonight.
answers: I would rather stay at home tonight.
items.explanation: 'Would rather' takes the bare infinitive.

items.sentence: Open the window and let some fresh air in, don't you?
answers: Open the window and let some fresh air in, will you?
Open the window and let some fresh air in, won't you?
Open the window and let some fresh air in, would you?
items.explanation: An imperative takes a tag such as 'will you?', 'won't you?' or 'would you?'.

items.sentence: I can't help to laugh at his jokes.
answers: I can't help laughing at his jokes.
items.explanation: 'Can't help' meaning 'cannot stop oneself' is followed by a gerund.

items.sentence: Don't let the opportunity to slip away this time.
answers: Don't let the opportunity slip away this time.
items.explanation: 'Let' + object takes the bare infinitive.

items.sentence: He prevented me to go out at night.
answers: He prevented me from going out at night.
items.explanation: 'Prevent' takes object + 'from' + gerund.

items.sentence: The old man has laid in bed for weeks.
answers: The old man has lain in bed for weeks.
items.explanation: The past participle of 'lie' (recline) is 'lain'.

items.sentence: The water pipes have froze in the cold night.
answers: The water pipes have frozen in the cold night.
items.explanation: The past participle of 'freeze' is 'frozen'.

items.sentence: The officer ordered the guard that he open the gate.
answers: The officer ordered the guard to open the gate.
items.explanation: Reported commands use 'order' + object + to-infinitive.

items.sentence: He used to smoking but has now quit.
answers: He used to smoke but has now quit.
items.explanation: Past habit 'used to' takes the base form, not a gerund.

items.sentence: The committee decided that the matter will be discussed at the next session.
answers: The committee decided that the matter would be discussed at the next session.
items.explanation: After a past main verb ('decided'), 'will' changes to 'would'.

items.sentence: She has written her first novel in 2010.
answers: She wrote her first novel in 2010.
items.explanation: A specific past date requires the past simple.

items.sentence: I know him since our school days in Sargodha.
answers: I have known him since our school days in Sargodha.
items.explanation: A state continuing from a past point up to now takes the present perfect with 'since'.

items.sentence: When the inspector arrived, the clerks already destroyed the files.
answers: When the inspector arrived, the clerks had already destroyed the files.
items.explanation: An action completed before another past action takes the past perfect.

items.sentence: By the time you will get this letter, I shall have left for Dubai.
answers: By the time you get this letter, I shall have left for Dubai.
items.explanation: 'By the time' introduces a time clause, which takes the present tense for future reference.

items.sentence: This book is consisting of twelve chapters and an appendix.
answers: This book consists of twelve chapters and an appendix.
items.explanation: 'Consist' describes a state and takes the simple present.

items.sentence: Does the train stops at Rohri on its way to Karachi?
answers: Does the train stop at Rohri on its way to Karachi?
items.explanation: In a question with 'does', the main verb has no -s ending.

items.sentence: The family is quarrelling among themselves over the property.
answers: The family are quarrelling among themselves over the property.
items.explanation: When members act separately (quarrelling among themselves), the collective noun takes a plural verb.

items.sentence: Measles are spreading in several districts of the province.
answers: Measles is spreading in several districts of the province.
items.explanation: Names of diseases ending in -s (measles, mumps) take a singular verb.

items.sentence: Either the father or his sons has to sign the document.
answers: Either the father or his sons have to sign the document.
items.explanation: The verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'sons', which is plural.

items.sentence: Nobody in the office were willing to work late.
answers: Nobody in the office was willing to work late.
items.explanation: 'Nobody' is singular and takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: Gold, as well as silver, have become expensive this year.
answers: Gold, as well as silver, has become expensive this year.
items.focus: Agreement: as well as, along with
items.explanation: The verb agrees with 'gold'; the phrase with 'as well as' is parenthetical.

items.sentence: The number of women in the workforce are growing steadily.
answers: The number of women in the workforce is growing steadily.
items.explanation: 'The number' is the singular head of the subject.

items.sentence: One of the reasons for the delay were the strike.
answers: One of the reasons for the delay was the strike.
items.explanation: The subject is 'one', so the verb is singular.

items.sentence: If he had left earlier, he would catch the train.
answers: If he had left earlier, he would have caught the train.
items.explanation: An unreal past condition requires 'would have' + past participle.

items.sentence: I wish it will stop raining before the wedding procession arrives.
answers: I wish it would stop raining before the wedding procession arrives.
items.explanation: 'Wish' about a desired change is followed by 'would', not 'will'.

items.sentence: It is high time that the authorities repair this road.
answers: It is high time that the authorities repaired this road.
items.explanation: After 'it is high time that', use the past simple.

items.sentence: No sooner the budget was presented than the opposition walked out.
answers: No sooner was the budget presented than the opposition walked out.
No sooner had the budget been presented than the opposition walked out.
items.explanation: A clause beginning with 'no sooner' needs subject-auxiliary inversion.

items.sentence: Scarcely the guests had arrived when the storm broke.
answers: Scarcely had the guests arrived when the storm broke.
items.explanation: An initial 'scarcely' requires the auxiliary to come before the subject.

items.sentence: The meeting was took place in the committee room.
answers: The meeting took place in the committee room.
items.explanation: 'Take place' is intransitive and has no passive form.

items.sentence: He dare not to oppose his father in front of guests.
answers: He dare not oppose his father in front of guests.
He does not dare to oppose his father in front of guests.
items.explanation: Modal 'dare not' is followed by the bare infinitive.

items.sentence: There is a post office near here, isn't it?
answers: There is a post office near here, isn't there?
items.explanation: When the sentence begins with 'there is', the tag repeats 'there'.

items.sentence: She promised helping me with my homework after dinner.
answers: She promised to help me with my homework after dinner.
items.explanation: 'Promise' takes a to-infinitive.

items.sentence: The teacher had the students to revise the chapter.
answers: The teacher had the students revise the chapter.
items.explanation: Causative 'have' + person is followed by the bare infinitive.

items.sentence: The doctor advised him taking a long holiday.
answers: The doctor advised him to take a long holiday.
items.explanation: 'Advise' + object is followed by a to-infinitive.

items.sentence: The workers are laying in the shade after lunch.
answers: The workers are lying in the shade after lunch.
items.explanation: 'Lie' (rest) has the -ing form 'lying'; 'laying' means putting something down.

items.sentence: He has wore the same coat for years.
answers: He has worn the same coat for years.
items.explanation: The past participle of 'wear' is 'worn'.

items.sentence: My mother asked me did I have my lunch.
answers: My mother asked me whether I had had my lunch.
My mother asked me if I had had my lunch.
items.explanation: A reported yes/no question uses 'whether' or 'if', statement word order and a backshifted tense.

items.sentence: You will soon get used to drive on the motorway.
answers: You will soon get used to driving on the motorway.
items.explanation: 'Get used to' is followed by a gerund.

items.sentence: The geography teacher explained that the Indus flowed into the Arabian Sea.
answers: The geography teacher explained that the Indus flows into the Arabian Sea.
items.explanation: A permanent fact or universal truth stays in the present tense even after a past reporting verb.

items.sentence: The factory has closed down in 2019 after heavy losses.
answers: The factory closed down in 2019 after heavy losses.
items.explanation: An action fixed at a past date ('in 2019') takes the past simple.

items.sentence: The patient has been in hospital since three days.
answers: The patient has been in hospital for three days.
items.explanation: 'Three days' is a length of time and takes 'for'.

items.sentence: The plane from Jeddah had landed ten minutes ago.
answers: The plane from Jeddah landed ten minutes ago.
items.explanation: 'Ago' is measured from now and takes the past simple, not the past perfect.

items.sentence: As long as the government will support farmers, production will rise.
answers: As long as the government supports farmers, production will rise.
items.explanation: Conditional and time clauses with 'as long as' take the present tense, not 'will'.

items.sentence: Most students are preferring online classes to crowded lecture halls nowadays.
answers: Most students prefer online classes to crowded lecture halls nowadays.
items.explanation: 'Prefer' is a stative verb of preference and is not used in the continuous.

items.sentence: Did you saw the eclipse from your rooftop last night?
answers: Did you see the eclipse from your rooftop last night?
items.explanation: After 'did', the main verb is in the base form.

items.sentence: The public is requested to keep their belongings safe.
answers: The public are requested to keep their belongings safe.
items.explanation: When 'the public' is thought of as individuals (shown by 'their'), the verb is plural.

items.sentence: The equipment in the laboratory have been replaced.
answers: The equipment in the laboratory has been replaced.
items.explanation: 'Equipment' is uncountable and takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: Not only the students but also the teacher were punished.
answers: Not only the students but also the teacher was punished.
items.explanation: With 'not only ... but also', the verb agrees with the nearer subject.

items.sentence: Each of the ministers were given a briefing on security.
answers: Each of the ministers was given a briefing on security.
items.explanation: 'Each of' is singular and takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: The chief guest, in addition to the other dignitaries, were welcomed warmly.
answers: The chief guest, in addition to the other dignitaries, was welcomed warmly.
items.focus: Agreement: as well as, along with
items.explanation: 'In addition to' does not make a singular subject plural.

items.sentence: A good number of tourists visits Swat every summer.
answers: A good number of tourists visit Swat every summer.
items.explanation: 'A good number of' means 'many' and takes a plural verb.

items.sentence: One of the main causes of inflation are the rising price of oil.
answers: One of the main causes of inflation is the rising price of oil.
items.explanation: The verb agrees with 'one', the head of the subject.

items.sentence: If we would leave now, we would reach Murree before dark.
answers: If we left now, we would reach Murree before dark.
If we leave now, we will reach Murree before dark.
items.explanation: 'Would' is not used in the if-clause; use the past simple (second conditional) or present simple (first conditional).

items.sentence: It is about time he finds a proper job.
answers: It is about time he found a proper job.
items.explanation: 'It is about time', like 'it is high time', takes the past simple.

items.sentence: No sooner did he saw the police than he ran away.
answers: No sooner did he see the police than he ran away.
items.explanation: After 'did', use the base form of the verb.

items.sentence: Hardly had the bridge been opened that cracks appeared in it.
answers: Hardly had the bridge been opened when cracks appeared in it.
Hardly had the bridge been opened before cracks appeared in it.
items.explanation: 'Hardly' is followed by 'when' or 'before', not 'that'.

items.sentence: The rioters were been arrested by the police.
answers: The rioters were arrested by the police.
The rioters have been arrested by the police.
items.explanation: 'Were been' is not a valid form; use the past passive 'were arrested' or the present perfect passive 'have been arrested'.

items.sentence: You should have inform the police at once.
answers: You should have informed the police at once.
items.explanation: 'Should have' is followed by the past participle.

items.sentence: He hardly ever comes on time, doesn't he?
answers: He hardly ever comes on time, does he?
items.explanation: 'Hardly' is negative in meaning, so the tag is positive.

items.sentence: He has given up to smoke on his doctor's advice.
answers: He has given up smoking on his doctor's advice.
items.explanation: 'Give up' is followed by a gerund.

items.sentence: I felt the ground to shake beneath my feet.
answers: I felt the ground shake beneath my feet.
I felt the ground shaking beneath my feet.
items.explanation: 'Feel' + object takes the bare infinitive or the -ing form.

items.sentence: She explained me the new rules of the hostel.
answers: She explained the new rules of the hostel to me.
items.explanation: 'Explain' does not take an indirect object directly; use 'explain something to someone'.

items.sentence: She sat the vase carefully on the table.
answers: She set the vase carefully on the table.
items.explanation: 'Set' (transitive) means 'place'; 'sit' does not take an object in this sense.

items.sentence: The principal told the students not make noise.
answers: The principal told the students not to make noise.
items.explanation: A reported negative command uses 'not to' + infinitive.

items.sentence: My grandfather is used to tell us stories every night.
answers: My grandfather used to tell us stories every night.
items.explanation: A past habit is expressed by 'used to' + base form, without 'is'.

items.sentence: Our elders taught us that honesty was the best policy.
answers: Our elders taught us that honesty is the best policy.
items.explanation: Proverbs and universal truths keep the present tense after a past main verb.

items.sentence: This is the first time I visit Gilgit.
answers: This is the first time I have visited Gilgit.
items.explanation: 'This is the first time' is followed by the present perfect.

items.sentence: We live in this house in Gulberg since 2015.
answers: We have lived in this house in Gulberg since 2015.
We have been living in this house in Gulberg since 2015.
items.explanation: With 'since' + starting point, the main verb must be in the present perfect, not the present simple.

items.sentence: The examination had started at nine and had ended at noon yesterday.
answers: The examination started at nine and ended at noon yesterday.
items.explanation: Past events told in sequence at stated times take the past simple; the past perfect is not needed without an earlier-past contrast.

items.sentence: Unless the rains will come soon, the crops will fail.
answers: Unless the rains come soon, the crops will fail.
items.explanation: A clause with 'unless' referring to the future takes the present tense.

items.sentence: The committee is wanting a detailed report by Friday.
answers: The committee wants a detailed report by Friday.
items.explanation: 'Want' expresses a state of desire and takes the simple form.

items.sentence: The office does not opens on Sundays or public holidays.
answers: The office does not open on Sundays or public holidays.
items.explanation: 'Does not' is followed by the base form of the verb.

items.sentence: The crew is unable to agree among themselves about the route.
answers: The crew are unable to agree among themselves about the route.
items.explanation: Disagreement 'among themselves' shows the members acting separately, so the collective noun takes a plural verb.

items.sentence: Ten kilometres are a long distance to walk in this heat.
answers: Ten kilometres is a long distance to walk in this heat.
items.explanation: A plural amount of distance, money or time treated as one quantity takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: Neither the medicine nor the injections has reduced his fever.
answers: Neither the medicine nor the injections have reduced his fever.
items.explanation: The verb agrees with the nearer subject, the plural 'injections'.

items.sentence: Every house in the street have a small garden.
answers: Every house in the street has a small garden.
items.explanation: 'Every' + singular noun takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: Ahmed, and not his friends, were responsible for the damage.
answers: Ahmed, and not his friends, was responsible for the damage.
items.focus: Agreement: as well as, along with
items.explanation: When a subject is followed by 'and not' + noun, the verb agrees with the affirmative subject.

items.sentence: The number of trees in the city are decreasing alarmingly.
answers: The number of trees in the city is decreasing alarmingly.
items.explanation: 'The number of' takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: One of her daughters are a judge in the High Court.
answers: One of her daughters is a judge in the High Court.
items.explanation: 'One of' + plural noun takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: Should you will need any help, please contact the front desk.
answers: Should you need any help, please contact the front desk.
items.explanation: Inverted 'should' in a condition is followed by the base form of the verb.

items.sentence: It is high time for the nation realised its potential.
answers: It is high time for the nation to realise its potential.
It is high time the nation realised its potential.
items.explanation: Use either 'for' + noun + to-infinitive or subject + past simple; the two patterns cannot be mixed.

items.sentence: No sooner had the curfew been lifted that the markets reopened.
answers: No sooner had the curfew been lifted than the markets reopened.
items.explanation: 'No sooner' is followed by 'than', not 'that'.

items.sentence: I had hardly sat down than the doorbell rang.
answers: I had hardly sat down when the doorbell rang.
I had hardly sat down before the doorbell rang.
items.explanation: Even without inversion, 'hardly' pairs with 'when' or 'before', not 'than'.

items.sentence: A new motorway is being construct between the two cities.
answers: A new motorway is being constructed between the two cities.
items.explanation: The continuous passive is 'is being' + past participle.

items.sentence: She must have went home early because she was not feeling well.
answers: She must have gone home early because she was not feeling well.
items.explanation: 'Must have' requires the past participle 'gone', not the past tense 'went'.

items.sentence: Your brother will attend the ceremony, isn't it?
answers: Your brother will attend the ceremony, won't he?
items.explanation: The tag repeats the auxiliary 'will' in its negative form with the pronoun 'he'.

items.sentence: The company hopes increasing its exports this year.
answers: The company hopes to increase its exports this year.
items.explanation: 'Hope' takes a to-infinitive.

items.sentence: Please let me to know your decision by Friday.
answers: Please let me know your decision by Friday.
items.explanation: 'Let' is followed by an object and the bare infinitive.

items.sentence: He objected to be called a coward by his colleagues.
answers: He objected to being called a coward by his colleagues.
items.explanation: In 'object to', 'to' is a preposition and is followed by a gerund.

items.sentence: The water level in the dam has raised after the rains.
answers: The water level in the dam has risen after the rains.
items.explanation: 'Rise' (intransitive) has the past participle 'risen'; 'raise' needs an object.

items.sentence: She asked whether I can lend her my notes.
answers: She asked whether I could lend her my notes.
items.explanation: After a past reporting verb, 'can' changes to 'could'.

items.sentence: She has got used to live alone since her husband died.
answers: She has got used to living alone since her husband died.
items.explanation: 'Get used to' takes a gerund.

items.sentence: Either of the two plans are acceptable to the board.
answers: Either of the two plans is acceptable to the board.
items.explanation: 'Either of' takes a singular verb.

items.sentence: Each of the twelve players have a role in the team.
answers: Each of the twelve players has a role in the team.
items.explanation: The subject is 'each', which is singular.

items.sentence: The ship, with its crew, were lost in the storm.
answers: The ship, with its crew, was lost in the storm.
items.focus: Agreement: as well as, along with
items.explanation: The verb agrees with the main subject, 'ship', not with the 'with' phrase.

items.sentence: If it had not rained, the match would be completed yesterday.
answers: If it had not rained, the match would have been completed yesterday.
items.explanation: A third conditional needs 'would have been' + past participle in the main clause.

items.sentence: It is high time the city has a proper sewerage system.
answers: It is high time the city had a proper sewerage system.
items.explanation: 'It is high time' requires the past simple in the following clause.

items.sentence: He was disappeared after the flood and was never seen again.
answers: He disappeared after the flood and was never seen again.
items.explanation: 'Disappear' is intransitive and cannot be made passive.

items.sentence: He might has missed the bus because of the traffic jam.
answers: He might have missed the bus because of the traffic jam.
items.explanation: After a modal, 'have' stays in the base form; 'has' is never used.

items.sentence: We should report this to the principal, isn't it?
answers: We should report this to the principal, shouldn't we?
items.explanation: The tag uses the same modal as the statement and the matching pronoun.

items.sentence: Please stop to talk while the lecture is going on.
answers: Please stop talking while the lecture is going on.
items.explanation: 'Stop' + gerund means to cease an activity; 'stop' + to-infinitive means to pause in order to do something.

items.sentence: The heavy rain made the river to overflow its banks.
answers: The heavy rain made the river overflow its banks.
items.explanation: Active 'make' + object takes the bare infinitive.

items.sentence: My father wants that I become a doctor.
answers: My father wants me to become a doctor.
items.explanation: 'Want' takes object + to-infinitive, not a that-clause.

items.sentence: Our hen has lain an egg every morning this week.
answers: Our hen has laid an egg every morning this week.
items.explanation: Producing an egg is 'lay', whose past participle is 'laid'.

items.sentence: Two days ago he said that he was going to Lahore tomorrow.
answers: Two days ago he said that he was going to Lahore the next day.
Two days ago he said that he was going to Lahore the following day.
items.explanation: When speech is reported later, 'tomorrow' changes to 'the next day' or 'the following day'.

items.sentence: There use to be a large banyan tree near the mosque.
answers: There used to be a large banyan tree near the mosque.
items.explanation: The affirmative past-habit form is 'used to'.

items.sentence: The officer was accused for embezzling funds from the provincial education budget.
answers: The officer was accused of embezzling funds from the provincial education budget.
items.explanation: 'Accuse' takes 'of' before the charge: accuse someone of something.

items.sentence: All government departments must comply to the new procurement rules from July.
answers: All government departments must comply with the new procurement rules from July.
items.explanation: 'Comply' is followed by 'with', not 'to'.

items.sentence: Many people abstain to food and drink from dawn to dusk during Ramadan.
answers: Many people abstain from food and drink from dawn to dusk during Ramadan.
items.explanation: 'Abstain' takes 'from'.

items.sentence: Farmers in lower Sindh depend over canal water for irrigating their fields.
answers: Farmers in lower Sindh depend on canal water for irrigating their fields.
Farmers in lower Sindh depend upon canal water for irrigating their fields.
items.explanation: 'Depend' is followed by 'on' or 'upon'.

items.sentence: The opposition insisted for an immediate inquiry into the rigging allegations.
answers: The opposition insisted on an immediate inquiry into the rigging allegations.
The opposition insisted upon an immediate inquiry into the rigging allegations.
items.explanation: 'Insist' takes 'on' or 'upon', not 'for'.

items.sentence: The landlord deprived the widow from her share of the inheritance.
answers: The landlord deprived the widow of her share of the inheritance.
items.explanation: 'Deprive' takes 'of': deprive someone of something.

items.sentence: The court acquitted the journalist from all the charges against him.
answers: The court acquitted the journalist of all the charges against him.
items.explanation: 'Acquit' takes 'of': acquit someone of a charge.

items.sentence: The doctor advised him to refrain of eating fried food after the surgery.
answers: The doctor advised him to refrain from eating fried food after the surgery.
items.explanation: 'Refrain' is followed by 'from'.

items.sentence: Her elderly father is suffering with a high fever and needs rest.
answers: Her elderly father is suffering from a high fever and needs rest.
items.explanation: An illness is something one suffers 'from'.

items.sentence: The smuggler was sentenced for seven years' rigorous imprisonment by the court.
answers: The smuggler was sentenced to seven years' rigorous imprisonment by the court.
items.explanation: One is sentenced 'to' a punishment ('for' introduces the crime).

items.sentence: She prefers reading novels than watching dramas on television.
answers: She prefers reading novels to watching dramas on television.
items.explanation: 'Prefer' one thing 'to' another, not 'than'.

items.sentence: The minister has not replied my letter about the closure of the school.
answers: The minister has not replied to my letter about the closure of the school.
items.explanation: 'Reply' is intransitive and needs 'to' before its object.

items.sentence: The villagers complained the district officer about the shortage of drinking water.
answers: The villagers complained to the district officer about the shortage of drinking water.
items.explanation: One complains 'to' a person 'about' a matter.

items.sentence: The prize money was divided between the six members of the winning team.
answers: The prize money was divided among the six members of the winning team.
The prize money was divided amongst the six members of the winning team.
items.explanation: 'Between' is used for two; 'among' for more than two.

items.sentence: I cannot agree to your view that the census figures were manipulated.
answers: I cannot agree with your view that the census figures were manipulated.
items.explanation: We agree 'with' a person or opinion and 'to' a proposal or terms.

items.sentence: The students were divided in four groups for the debate competition.
answers: The students were divided into four groups for the debate competition.
items.explanation: Something is divided 'into' parts.

items.sentence: She was so absorbed with her novel that she did not hear the doorbell.
answers: She was so absorbed in her novel that she did not hear the doorbell.
items.explanation: 'Absorbed' (deeply occupied) takes 'in'.

items.sentence: The committee was not satisfied from the explanation given by the contractor.
answers: The committee was not satisfied with the explanation given by the contractor.
items.explanation: 'Satisfied' is followed by 'with'.

items.sentence: The professor is well acquainted about the history of the Mughal Empire.
answers: The professor is well acquainted with the history of the Mughal Empire.
items.explanation: 'Acquainted' takes 'with'.

items.sentence: Sialkot is famous by its surgical instruments and sports goods.
answers: Sialkot is famous for its surgical instruments and sports goods.
items.explanation: A place is famous 'for' something.

items.sentence: Balochistan is rich of minerals such as copper, gold and natural gas.
answers: Balochistan is rich in minerals such as copper, gold and natural gas.
items.explanation: 'Rich' meaning well supplied takes 'in'.

items.sentence: Young children are often afraid from the dark and from loud noises.
answers: Young children are often afraid of the dark and of loud noises.
items.explanation: 'Afraid' takes 'of'; both parallel phrases need 'of'.

items.sentence: He was jealous from his cousin's success in the competitive examination.
answers: He was jealous of his cousin's success in the competitive examination.
items.explanation: 'Jealous' is followed by 'of'.

items.sentence: The headmaster was angry upon the boy for breaking the laboratory window.
answers: The headmaster was angry with the boy for breaking the laboratory window.
items.explanation: We are angry 'with' a person and 'at' or 'about' a thing.

items.sentence: My younger sister is very good in mathematics but weak in languages.
answers: My younger sister is very good at mathematics but weak in languages.
items.explanation: 'Good' meaning skilful takes 'at'.

items.sentence: He felt ashamed for his rude behaviour towards his teacher.
answers: He felt ashamed of his rude behaviour towards his teacher.
items.explanation: 'Ashamed' is followed by 'of'.

items.sentence: Our grandmother is very fond with green tea and old Urdu ghazals.
answers: Our grandmother is very fond of green tea and old Urdu ghazals.
items.explanation: 'Fond' takes 'of'.

items.sentence: Many young people today are addicted with their mobile phones.
answers: Many young people today are addicted to their mobile phones.
items.explanation: 'Addicted' is followed by 'to'.

items.sentence: The success of the wheat crop is entirely dependent of timely rainfall.
answers: The success of the wheat crop is entirely dependent on timely rainfall.
The success of the wheat crop is entirely dependent upon timely rainfall.
items.explanation: 'Dependent' takes 'on' or 'upon' ('independent of' takes 'of').

items.sentence: The tourists were deeply impressed from the hospitality of the people of Hunza.
answers: The tourists were deeply impressed by the hospitality of the people of Hunza.
The tourists were deeply impressed with the hospitality of the people of Hunza.
items.explanation: 'Impressed' takes 'by' or 'with', not 'from'.

items.sentence: The new tax policy is quite different than the one announced last year.
answers: The new tax policy is quite different from the one announced last year.
The new tax policy is quite different to the one announced last year.
items.explanation: In British English 'different' is followed by 'from' (or 'to'), not 'than'.

items.sentence: I have full faith on the judiciary to deliver a fair verdict.
answers: I have full faith in the judiciary to deliver a fair verdict.
items.explanation: 'Faith' and 'confidence' take 'in'.

items.sentence: He has no confidence on his own ability to speak in public.
answers: He has no confidence in his own ability to speak in public.
items.explanation: 'Confidence' is followed by 'in'.

items.sentence: The government has laid great emphasis over primary education this year.
answers: The government has laid great emphasis on primary education this year.
items.explanation: The noun 'emphasis' takes 'on'.

items.sentence: She has a natural aptitude in learning foreign languages.
answers: She has a natural aptitude for learning foreign languages.
items.explanation: 'Aptitude' is followed by 'for'.

items.sentence: She takes great pride on her work as a district health officer.
answers: She takes great pride in her work as a district health officer.
items.explanation: 'Take pride' is followed by 'in'.

items.sentence: The candidates were told to write their answers with ink, not pencil.
answers: The candidates were told to write their answers in ink, not pencil.
The candidates were told to write their answers in ink, not in pencil.
items.explanation: We write 'in' ink or 'in' pencil (the medium), but 'with' a pen.

items.sentence: There has been a sharp increase of the price of petrol this month.
answers: There has been a sharp increase in the price of petrol this month.
items.explanation: 'Increase' and 'decrease' are followed by 'in' when naming what changes.

items.sentence: The minister refused to give any answer of the journalist's question.
answers: The minister refused to give any answer to the journalist's question.
items.explanation: The noun 'answer' takes 'to'.

items.sentence: The Karachi Express reached at Lahore two hours behind schedule.
answers: The Karachi Express reached Lahore two hours behind schedule.
items.explanation: 'Reach' is transitive and takes a direct object without 'at'.

items.sentence: The hospital administration ordered for fresh supplies of insulin last week.
answers: The hospital administration ordered fresh supplies of insulin last week.
items.explanation: 'Order' takes a direct object; 'for' is not needed.

items.sentence: The inspector entered into the room without knocking on the door.
answers: The inspector entered the room without knocking on the door.
items.explanation: 'Enter' a place takes a direct object; 'enter into' is used for agreements or discussions.

items.sentence: Before signing the contract, we must consider about all the risks involved.
answers: Before signing the contract, we must consider all the risks involved.
items.explanation: 'Consider' is transitive and takes no preposition.

items.sentence: The witness described about the accident in great detail before the magistrate.
answers: The witness described the accident in great detail before the magistrate.
items.explanation: 'Describe' takes a direct object; 'about' is wrong.

items.sentence: In appearance she closely resembles to her late grandmother.
answers: In appearance she closely resembles her late grandmother.
items.explanation: 'Resemble' is transitive and takes no preposition.

items.sentence: The troops attacked on the enemy post just before dawn.
answers: The troops attacked the enemy post just before dawn.
items.explanation: The verb 'attack' takes a direct object (compare the noun: 'an attack on').

items.sentence: Please mention about your previous experience in the covering letter.
answers: Please mention your previous experience in the covering letter.
items.explanation: 'Mention' is transitive; 'about' is not used after it.

items.sentence: The speaker emphasised on the need for population control in Pakistan.
answers: The speaker emphasised the need for population control in Pakistan.
items.explanation: The verb 'emphasise' takes a direct object; only the noun 'emphasis' takes 'on'.

items.sentence: My father will accompany with me to the passport office tomorrow.
answers: My father will accompany me to the passport office tomorrow.
items.explanation: 'Accompany' takes a direct object without 'with'.

items.sentence: The clerk has requested for a transfer to his home district.
answers: The clerk has requested a transfer to his home district.
items.explanation: The verb 'request' takes a direct object; only the noun takes 'for' ('a request for').

items.sentence: Please answer to all the questions in the first section of the paper.
answers: Please answer all the questions in the first section of the paper.
items.explanation: The verb 'answer' is transitive (compare the noun: 'an answer to').

items.sentence: The new recruit lacks in the experience required for this sensitive post.
answers: The new recruit lacks the experience required for this sensitive post.
items.explanation: The verb 'lack' takes a direct object; 'lacking in' is used only with the adjective form.

items.sentence: After the long journey from Gilgit, we returned to home late at night.
answers: After the long journey from Gilgit, we returned home late at night.
items.explanation: 'Home' used as an adverb after verbs of motion takes no 'to'.

items.sentence: The committee will investigate into the causes of the factory fire.
answers: The committee will investigate the causes of the factory fire.
items.explanation: 'Investigate' is transitive; 'into' belongs with 'inquire' or 'look'.

items.sentence: He has always been a honest officer who never accepted a bribe.
answers: He has always been an honest officer who never accepted a bribe.
items.explanation: 'An' is used before a vowel sound; the 'h' in 'honest' is silent.

items.sentence: She was awarded an one-year scholarship to study public policy in London.
answers: She was awarded a one-year scholarship to study public policy in London.
items.explanation: 'One' begins with a consonant sound /w/, so it takes 'a'.

items.sentence: Allama Iqbal earned his doctorate at an European university.
answers: Allama Iqbal earned his doctorate at a European university.
items.explanation: 'European' begins with the consonant sound /j/, so it takes 'a'.

items.sentence: He has a MPhil in economics from Quaid-i-Azam University.
answers: He has an MPhil in economics from Quaid-i-Azam University.
items.explanation: 'MPhil' is pronounced with an initial vowel sound /em/, so it takes 'an'.

items.sentence: Ravi flows past the city of Lahore before joining the Chenab.
answers: The Ravi flows past the city of Lahore before joining the Chenab.
items.explanation: Names of rivers take the definite article.

items.sentence: Himalayas form a natural barrier along the northern border of the subcontinent.
answers: The Himalayas form a natural barrier along the northern border of the subcontinent.
