items.explanation: Names of mountain ranges take 'the'.

items.sentence: The honesty and the hard work are the keys to success in public life.
answers: Honesty and hard work are the keys to success in public life.
items.explanation: Abstract nouns used in a general sense take no article.

items.sentence: The gold has become too expensive for most families to buy for weddings.
answers: Gold has become too expensive for most families to buy for weddings.
items.explanation: Material nouns used in a general sense take no article.

items.sentence: Shoaib is best batsman in our college cricket team this season.
answers: Shoaib is the best batsman in our college cricket team this season.
items.explanation: A superlative adjective normally takes 'the'.

items.sentence: My younger brother is studying hard to become engineer.
answers: My younger brother is studying hard to become an engineer.
items.explanation: A singular countable noun of profession needs an article: 'an engineer'.

items.sentence: Most of the boys in our street play the cricket every Sunday morning.
answers: Most of the boys in our street play cricket every Sunday morning.
items.explanation: Names of games and sports take no article.

items.sentence: We came from Rawalpindi to Peshawar by the train last night.
answers: We came from Rawalpindi to Peshawar by train last night.
items.explanation: 'By' + means of transport takes no article: by train, by bus, by air.

items.sentence: What a pleasant weather we are having in Islamabad this week!
answers: What pleasant weather we are having in Islamabad this week!
items.explanation: 'Weather' is uncountable, so it cannot take 'a'.

items.sentence: The hall looked almost empty because only few students attended the lecture.
answers: The hall looked almost empty because only a few students attended the lecture.
items.explanation: 'Only' combines with 'a few' (some, a small number); 'few' alone means hardly any.

items.sentence: Arabian Sea forms the southern border of Pakistan along the Makran coast.
answers: The Arabian Sea forms the southern border of Pakistan along the Makran coast.
items.explanation: Names of seas and oceans take 'the'.

items.sentence: The Prime Minister left for the Saudi Arabia on an official visit.
answers: The Prime Minister left for Saudi Arabia on an official visit.
items.explanation: Most country names take no article (exceptions include names with 'Republic', 'Kingdom' or plural forms).

items.sentence: He usually goes to the bed at ten and wakes up before Fajr.
answers: He usually goes to bed at ten and wakes up before Fajr.
items.explanation: In set phrases such as 'go to bed', 'go to school' and 'go to work', no article is used.

items.sentence: She left home without the breakfast because she was late for the exam.
answers: She left home without breakfast because she was late for the exam.
items.explanation: Names of meals used in a general sense take no article.

items.sentence: My elder brother is far more patient than me when dealing with customers.
answers: My elder brother is far more patient than I when dealing with customers.
My elder brother is far more patient than I am when dealing with customers.
items.explanation: In formal English the pronoun after 'than' takes the case it would have in the understood clause: 'than I (am)'.

items.sentence: Let you and I prepare the budget proposal before the meeting.
answers: Let you and me prepare the budget proposal before the meeting.
items.explanation: 'Let' is followed by the objective case: 'let you and me'.

items.sentence: The first prize was shared by Ahmed and I in the inter-college debate.
answers: The first prize was shared by Ahmed and me in the inter-college debate.
items.explanation: A pronoun after a preposition ('by') must be in the objective case.

items.sentence: Us students were not informed about the change in the examination schedule.
answers: We students were not informed about the change in the examination schedule.
items.explanation: The pronoun is part of the subject, so the subjective 'we' is needed.

items.sentence: The principal called Sara and I to his office after the assembly.
answers: The principal called Sara and me to his office after the assembly.
items.explanation: The pronoun is an object of 'called', so 'me' is required.

items.sentence: Me and my friend went to the British Council library to borrow books.
answers: My friend and I went to the British Council library to borrow books.
items.explanation: A subject pronoun must be 'I', and courtesy places the first person last.

items.sentence: Nobody except he knew the combination of the office safe.
answers: Nobody except him knew the combination of the office safe.
items.explanation: 'Except' is a preposition, so the pronoun after it takes the objective case.

items.sentence: This dispute is strictly between he and his former business partner.
answers: This dispute is strictly between him and his former business partner.
items.explanation: 'Between' is a preposition and must be followed by the objective case.

items.sentence: My sister is not as tall as him, though she is older.
answers: My sister is not as tall as he, though she is older.
My sister is not as tall as he is, though she is older.
items.explanation: In formal English the pronoun after 'as…as' takes the case it has in the understood clause: 'as he (is)'.

items.sentence: The manager asked my colleague and I to stay late on Friday.
answers: The manager asked my colleague and me to stay late on Friday.
items.explanation: The pronoun is an object of 'asked', so the objective 'me' is needed.

items.sentence: The teacher gave the extra books to we girls who sat in the front row.
answers: The teacher gave the extra books to us girls who sat in the front row.
items.explanation: After the preposition 'to' the objective 'us' is required.

items.sentence: He absented from the office for three days without informing anyone.
answers: He absented himself from the office for three days without informing anyone.
items.explanation: 'Absent' as a verb is always used reflexively: absent oneself.

items.sentence: My colleague and myself will represent the department at the seminar.
answers: My colleague and I will represent the department at the seminar.
items.explanation: A reflexive pronoun cannot stand as a subject; use 'I'.

items.sentence: Please send the revised documents directly to myself by Monday.
answers: Please send the revised documents directly to me by Monday.
items.explanation: A reflexive pronoun is used only when it refers back to the subject; here 'me' is required.

items.sentence: The children enjoyed very much at the Lok Virsa festival.
answers: The children enjoyed themselves very much at the Lok Virsa festival.
items.explanation: 'Enjoy' needs an object; when it means 'have a good time', the reflexive is used.

items.sentence: She availed of the opportunity to study abroad on a government scholarship.
answers: She availed herself of the opportunity to study abroad on a government scholarship.
items.explanation: 'Avail' in this sense is reflexive: avail oneself of something.

items.sentence: He prides on his punctuality and has never been late for work.
answers: He prides himself on his punctuality and has never been late for work.
items.explanation: The verb 'pride' is used reflexively: pride oneself on something.

items.sentence: Your brother and yourself are invited to the dinner at the Governor House.
answers: Your brother and you are invited to the dinner at the Governor House.
items.explanation: 'Yourself' cannot be a subject; the personal pronoun 'you' is needed.

items.sentence: The candidate who the committee selected has declined the offer.
answers: The candidate whom the committee selected has declined the offer.
items.explanation: The pronoun is the object of 'selected', so 'whom' is required.

items.sentence: Whom is responsible for the delay in releasing the funds?
answers: Who is responsible for the delay in releasing the funds?
items.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of 'is', so 'who' is required.

items.sentence: To who should I address my application for the post of lecturer?
answers: To whom should I address my application for the post of lecturer?
items.explanation: After a preposition the objective form 'whom' is used.

items.sentence: The man whom I thought was honest cheated the whole village.
answers: The man who I thought was honest cheated the whole village.
items.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of 'was'; 'I thought' is a parenthetical insertion.

items.sentence: He is the officer whom, I believe, will head the new commission.
answers: He is the officer who, I believe, will head the new commission.
items.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of 'will head', so 'who' is correct.

items.sentence: The prize should go to whomever deserves it most, not to a favourite.
answers: The prize should go to whoever deserves it most, not to a favourite.
items.explanation: The pronoun is the subject of 'deserves', so 'whoever' is needed even after 'to'.

items.sentence: The scholar to who the award was presented teaches at Government College.
answers: The scholar to whom the award was presented teaches at Government College.
items.explanation: After a preposition the relative pronoun takes the objective form 'whom'.

items.sentence: Who did the President appoint as the new ambassador to China?
answers: Whom did the President appoint as the new ambassador to China?
items.explanation: In formal English the object of 'appoint' takes 'whom'.

items.sentence: The doctor which treated my mother has been transferred to Quetta.
answers: The doctor who treated my mother has been transferred to Quetta.
The doctor that treated my mother has been transferred to Quetta.
items.explanation: 'Which' refers to things; 'who' (or 'that') is used for people.

items.sentence: The students which failed the test will be given another chance.
answers: The students who failed the test will be given another chance.
The students that failed the test will be given another chance.
items.explanation: Use 'who' or 'that', not 'which', for people.

items.sentence: One should always respect his elders and keep his promises.
answers: One should always respect one's elders and keep one's promises.
items.explanation: Once 'one' is used as the subject, formal British English continues with 'one's'.

items.sentence: One must do your duty regardless of the consequences.
answers: One must do one's duty regardless of the consequences.
items.explanation: 'One' must not be followed by 'you' or 'your'; keep 'one's'.

items.sentence: Each of the boys has brought their own lunch box on the trip.
answers: Each of the boys has brought his own lunch box on the trip.
items.explanation: 'Each' is singular, and the antecedent is all male, so 'his' is required.

items.sentence: Every one of the girls submitted their assignment before the deadline.
answers: Every one of the girls submitted her assignment before the deadline.
items.explanation: 'Every one' is singular; with an all-female group the pronoun is 'her'.

items.sentence: Neither of the brothers has paid their share of the electricity bill.
answers: Neither of the brothers has paid his share of the electricity bill.
items.explanation: 'Neither' is singular, so the possessive must be singular: 'his'.

items.sentence: Either of the girls can lend you their notes on the Mughal period.
answers: Either of the girls can lend you her notes on the Mughal period.
items.explanation: 'Either' is singular; for a female antecedent use 'her'.

items.sentence: If one works hard and stays honest, you will surely succeed.
answers: If one works hard and stays honest, one will surely succeed.
items.explanation: Do not switch from 'one' to 'you' within a sentence.

items.sentence: Although she studied abroad, she does not speak French very good.
answers: Although she studied abroad, she does not speak French very well.
items.explanation: A verb is modified by an adverb: 'well', not the adjective 'good'.

items.sentence: The new traffic policy was implemented so bad that it caused chaos.
answers: The new traffic policy was implemented so badly that it caused chaos.
items.explanation: The verb 'implemented' needs the adverb 'badly'.

items.sentence: He looked very sadly after hearing the news of his friend's death.
answers: He looked very sad after hearing the news of his friend's death.
items.explanation: Linking verbs such as 'look', 'seem' and 'feel' take an adjective complement.

items.sentence: The roses in the Shalimar Gardens smell very sweetly in spring.
answers: The roses in the Shalimar Gardens smell very sweet in spring.
items.explanation: 'Smell' as a linking verb is followed by an adjective.

items.sentence: The officer spoke very rude to the clerk in front of the visitors.
answers: The officer spoke very rudely to the clerk in front of the visitors.
items.explanation: The verb 'spoke' is modified by the adverb 'rudely'.

items.sentence: She was real happy with her result in the provincial board examination.
answers: She was really happy with her result in the provincial board examination.
items.explanation: An adjective ('happy') is modified by an adverb: 'really', not 'real'.

items.sentence: Bus drivers often drive too fastly on the GT Road at night.
answers: Bus drivers often drive too fast on the GT Road at night.
items.explanation: 'Fast' is both adjective and adverb; 'fastly' does not exist.

items.sentence: The milk left outside the fridge overnight tasted sourly in the morning.
answers: The milk left outside the fridge overnight tasted sour in the morning.
items.explanation: 'Taste' as a linking verb takes an adjective complement.

items.sentence: He came lately to the meeting and missed the minister's briefing.
answers: He came late to the meeting and missed the minister's briefing.
items.explanation: 'Late' means 'after the expected time'; 'lately' means 'recently'.

items.sentence: I feel very badly about missing your sister's wedding last week.
answers: I feel very bad about missing your sister's wedding last week.
items.explanation: 'Feel' is a linking verb and takes an adjective: 'feel bad'.

items.sentence: The labourer works hardly from morning till evening to feed his family.
answers: The labourer works hard from morning till evening to feed his family.
items.explanation: 'Hard' is the adverb meaning 'with effort'; 'hardly' means 'scarcely'.

items.sentence: The new bridge was near complete when the funds suddenly ran out.
answers: The new bridge was nearly complete when the funds suddenly ran out.
items.explanation: 'Nearly' (almost) is the adverb needed to modify 'complete'.

items.sentence: After the operation the patient is doing good and will be discharged soon.
answers: After the operation the patient is doing well and will be discharged soon.
items.explanation: Referring to health or progress, the adverb 'well' is used after 'doing'.

items.sentence: The candidate answered the interview questions confident and clearly.
answers: The candidate answered the interview questions confidently and clearly.
items.explanation: Both words modify 'answered', so both must be adverbs.

items.sentence: This is the most cheapest flight available from Lahore to Jeddah.
answers: This is the cheapest flight available from Lahore to Jeddah.
items.explanation: A superlative already formed with '-est' must not take 'most'.

items.sentence: Imran is more taller than his elder brother.
answers: Imran is taller than his elder brother.
items.explanation: 'Taller' is already comparative; 'more' is redundant.

items.sentence: The situation in the flood-hit areas is more worse than last year.
answers: The situation in the flood-hit areas is worse than last year.
items.explanation: 'Worse' is already the comparative of 'bad'; do not add 'more'.

items.sentence: Of the two plans submitted to the cabinet, this is the best.
answers: Of the two plans submitted to the cabinet, this is the better.
items.explanation: When only two things are compared, the comparative is used, not the superlative.

items.sentence: He is the strongest of the two brothers.
answers: He is the stronger of the two brothers.
items.explanation: For a comparison between two, use the comparative degree.

items.sentence: Which is the better of these three routes to Murree?
answers: Which is the best of these three routes to Murree?
items.explanation: For more than two, use the superlative degree.

items.sentence: Iqbal was greater than any poet of his age in the subcontinent.
answers: Iqbal was greater than any other poet of his age in the subcontinent.
items.explanation: When comparing one member with the rest of its own group, use 'any other'; otherwise he is compared with himself.

items.sentence: K2 is higher than any peak in the Karakoram range.
answers: K2 is higher than any other peak in the Karakoram range.
items.explanation: K2 belongs to the Karakoram, so the comparison needs 'any other'.

items.sentence: The climate of Murree is much cooler than Lahore.
answers: The climate of Murree is much cooler than that of Lahore.
items.explanation: Compare like with like: the climate of Murree with the climate ('that') of Lahore.

items.sentence: The population of Karachi is larger than Lahore.
answers: The population of Karachi is larger than that of Lahore.
items.explanation: A population must be compared with a population, so 'that of' is needed.

items.sentence: The salary of a schoolteacher is much lower than a bank manager.
answers: The salary of a schoolteacher is much lower than that of a bank manager.
items.explanation: Compare salary with salary: 'than that of a bank manager'.

items.sentence: Lahore is one of the oldest city in South Asia.
answers: Lahore is one of the oldest cities in South Asia.
items.explanation: 'One of the' + superlative is followed by a plural noun.

items.sentence: Village life is more preferable to city life for many retired people.
answers: Village life is preferable to city life for many retired people.
items.explanation: 'Preferable' already expresses comparison and does not take 'more'.

items.sentence: The new irrigation method is superior than the traditional flood system.
answers: The new irrigation method is superior to the traditional flood system.
items.explanation: Latin comparatives ending in '-ior' take 'to', not 'than'.

items.sentence: She is junior than me by two years in the Foreign Service.
answers: She is junior to me by two years in the Foreign Service.
items.explanation: 'Junior' is followed by 'to', not 'than'.

items.sentence: The meeting was held prior than the announcement of the federal budget.
answers: The meeting was held prior to the announcement of the federal budget.
items.explanation: 'Prior' takes 'to'.

items.sentence: Locally made cloth is no longer inferior than imported cloth.
answers: Locally made cloth is no longer inferior to imported cloth.
items.explanation: 'Inferior' takes 'to', not 'than'.

items.sentence: The new model is more superior to the old one in fuel efficiency.
answers: The new model is superior to the old one in fuel efficiency.
items.explanation: 'Superior' is already comparative and must not take 'more'.

items.sentence: The deputy commissioner is senior than the assistant commissioner in rank.
answers: The deputy commissioner is senior to the assistant commissioner in rank.
items.explanation: 'Senior' takes 'to', not 'than'.

items.sentence: Ahmed is three years elder than his sister, who works in Karachi.
answers: Ahmed is three years older than his sister, who works in Karachi.
items.explanation: 'Elder' is not used with 'than'; use 'older than' for comparison.

items.sentence: The Badshahi Mosque is one of the eldest buildings in Lahore.
answers: The Badshahi Mosque is one of the oldest buildings in Lahore.
items.explanation: 'Elder' and 'eldest' are used only for people in a family; for things use 'older', 'oldest'.

items.sentence: The city of Taxila is far elder than Islamabad.
answers: The city of Taxila is far older than Islamabad.
items.explanation: 'Elder' applies to related persons only and does not take 'than'; use 'older'.

items.sentence: Less people use public transport in Islamabad than in Karachi.
answers: Fewer people use public transport in Islamabad than in Karachi.
items.explanation: 'Fewer' is used with countable plural nouns; 'less' with uncountable nouns.

items.sentence: Our office received less complaints this month than last month.
answers: Our office received fewer complaints this month than last month.
items.explanation: 'Complaints' is countable, so 'fewer' is required.

items.sentence: There is fewer water in Tarbela Dam this year because of low rainfall.
answers: There is less water in Tarbela Dam this year because of low rainfall.
items.explanation: 'Water' is uncountable, so 'less' is required.

items.sentence: The new hybrid car uses fewer fuel than the old model.
answers: The new hybrid car uses less fuel than the old model.
items.explanation: 'Fuel' is uncountable and takes 'less'.

items.sentence: There is too many traffic on the Mall Road in the evening.
answers: There is too much traffic on the Mall Road in the evening.
items.explanation: 'Much' is used with uncountable nouns like 'traffic'; 'many' with countable plurals.

items.sentence: He does not have much friends since he moved to Quetta.
answers: He does not have many friends since he moved to Quetta.
items.explanation: 'Friends' is a countable plural, so 'many' is needed.

items.sentence: I have not got many time to spare before the examination.
answers: I have not got much time to spare before the examination.
items.explanation: 'Time' in this sense is uncountable, so 'much' is used.

items.sentence: Could you please repeat again the last part of your answer?
answers: Could you please repeat the last part of your answer?
items.explanation: 'Repeat' already means 'say again'; 'again' is redundant.

items.sentence: The two prime ministers met together on the sidelines of the summit.
answers: The two prime ministers met on the sidelines of the summit.
items.explanation: 'Met' already implies coming together; 'together' adds nothing.

items.sentence: After a few months of discipline, he reverted back to his old habits.
answers: After a few months of discipline, he reverted to his old habits.
items.explanation: 'Revert' means 'go back', so 'back' is redundant.

items.sentence: Let us all cooperate together to keep our neighbourhood clean.
answers: Let us all cooperate to keep our neighbourhood clean.
items.explanation: 'Cooperate' means 'work together'; 'together' is redundant.

items.sentence: The reason why he resigned is because he was unwell.
answers: The reason why he resigned is that he was unwell.
The reason he resigned is that he was unwell.
items.explanation: 'The reason… is because' repeats the idea of cause; use 'the reason… is that'.

items.sentence: The past history of Balochistan is full of tribal conflicts.
answers: The history of Balochistan is full of tribal conflicts.
items.explanation: History is by definition the past, so 'past' is redundant.

items.sentence: In my own personal opinion, the reforms came far too late.
answers: In my personal opinion, the reforms came far too late.
In my own opinion, the reforms came far too late.
items.explanation: 'Own' and 'personal' say the same thing; one is enough.

items.sentence: The troops advanced forward towards the border under heavy fire.
answers: The troops advanced towards the border under heavy fire.
items.explanation: 'Advance' already means 'move forward'.

items.sentence: Every customer who spends five thousand rupees will receive a free gift.
answers: Every customer who spends five thousand rupees will receive a gift.
items.explanation: A gift is free by definition, so 'free' is redundant.

items.sentence: The two proposals are equally alike in their aims and methods.
answers: The two proposals are alike in their aims and methods.
items.explanation: 'Alike' already expresses equality; 'equally' is superfluous.

items.sentence: The ATM machine outside the bank has been out of order for a week.
answers: The ATM outside the bank has been out of order for a week.
items.explanation: 'ATM' stands for 'automated teller machine', so 'machine' repeats itself.

items.sentence: The award for his novel came as an unexpected surprise to him.
answers: The award for his novel came as a surprise to him.
items.explanation: A surprise is unexpected by nature, so 'unexpected' is redundant.

items.sentence: The end result of the long negotiations was a modest pay rise.
answers: The result of the long negotiations was a modest pay rise.
items.explanation: 'Result' already means the end outcome.

items.sentence: He returned back from Dubai after working there for six years.
answers: He returned from Dubai after working there for six years.
items.explanation: 'Return' means 'come back'; 'back' is redundant.

items.sentence: The students assembled together in the main hall for the farewell party.
answers: The students assembled in the main hall for the farewell party.
items.explanation: 'Assemble' already means 'come together'.

items.sentence: My father, he is a retired professor of history at Government College.
answers: My father is a retired professor of history at Government College.
items.explanation: The pronoun 'he' needlessly repeats the subject 'my father'.

items.sentence: Do you know what time does the last train to Rawalpindi leave?
answers: Do you know what time the last train to Rawalpindi leaves?
items.explanation: In an embedded question the auxiliary 'does' is dropped and the subject precedes the verb.

items.sentence: I wonder why did the chairman resign so suddenly.
answers: I wonder why the chairman resigned so suddenly.
items.explanation: Embedded questions use statement word order and drop the auxiliary 'did'.

items.sentence: Please tell me when will the results of the written test be announced.
answers: Please tell me when the results of the written test will be announced.
items.explanation: In an indirect question the subject precedes the auxiliary.

items.sentence: Could you tell me where is the passport office in this city?
answers: Could you tell me where the passport office is in this city?
Could you tell me where the passport office in this city is?
items.explanation: An embedded question takes statement order: subject before verb.

items.sentence: My grandfather goes often to the mosque for the dawn prayer.
answers: My grandfather often goes to the mosque for the dawn prayer.
items.explanation: Adverbs of frequency come before the main verb.

items.sentence: She speaks very well English but finds French difficult.
answers: She speaks English very well but finds French difficult.
items.explanation: An adverb does not separate a verb from its direct object.

items.sentence: I have visited twice the Lahore Museum since I moved to the city.
answers: I have visited the Lahore Museum twice since I moved to the city.
items.explanation: An adverb like 'twice' should not separate a verb from its object; it follows the object.

items.sentence: Not only he speaks Urdu fluently but also Punjabi and Sindhi.
answers: He speaks not only Urdu but also Punjabi and Sindhi fluently.
He speaks fluently not only Urdu but also Punjabi and Sindhi.
items.explanation: 'Not only' must stand directly before the first of the two parallel items, matching 'but also'.

items.sentence: She not only visited Lahore but also Karachi during her stay.
answers: She visited not only Lahore but also Karachi during her stay.
items.explanation: 'Not only… but also' must precede parallel elements: 'not only Lahore but also Karachi'.

items.sentence: He not only is a renowned poet but also a gifted philosopher.
answers: He is not only a renowned poet but also a gifted philosopher.
items.explanation: Place 'not only' before the first of the two parallel complements, after the verb 'is'.

items.sentence: The trainer always is annoyed when the new recruits arrive late.
answers: The trainer is always annoyed when the new recruits arrive late.
items.explanation: Adverbs of frequency come after the verb 'be', not before it.

items.sentence: He has finished already the report on rural health facilities.
answers: He has already finished the report on rural health facilities.
items.explanation: 'Already' normally comes between the auxiliary and the main verb.

items.sentence: Seldom I have seen such dedication in a young civil servant.
answers: Seldom have I seen such dedication in a young civil servant.
items.explanation: When a negative adverb like 'seldom' begins a sentence, the auxiliary comes before the subject.

items.sentence: Never I had heard such a moving speech in the National Assembly.
answers: Never had I heard such a moving speech in the National Assembly.
items.explanation: Initial 'never' requires inversion of subject and auxiliary.

items.sentence: Rarely she visits her village now that she lives in Islamabad.
answers: Rarely does she visit her village now that she lives in Islamabad.
She rarely visits her village now that she lives in Islamabad.
items.explanation: A sentence opening with 'rarely' needs inversion with 'does'; alternatively move 'rarely' before the verb.

items.sentence: Only after the floods the government realised the need for new dams.
answers: Only after the floods did the government realise the need for new dams.
items.explanation: 'Only after' at the start of a sentence triggers inversion with an auxiliary.

items.sentence: Not a single word he said in his own defence before the tribunal.
answers: Not a single word did he say in his own defence before the tribunal.
He did not say a single word in his own defence before the tribunal.
items.explanation: A fronted negative object ('not a single word') requires auxiliary–subject inversion.

items.sentence: He passed out from the University of the Punjab in 2015 with distinction.
answers: He graduated from the University of the Punjab in 2015 with distinction.
items.explanation: In standard English 'pass out' means 'faint'; finishing university is 'graduate'.

items.sentence: Do one thing, call the electrician first thing tomorrow morning.
answers: Call the electrician first thing tomorrow morning.
Please do this: call the electrician first thing tomorrow morning.
items.explanation: 'Do one thing' is a literal translation not used in standard English; give the instruction directly.

items.sentence: My uncle is having three houses in the Defence area of Lahore.
answers: My uncle has three houses in the Defence area of Lahore.
items.explanation: 'Have' meaning 'possess' is a stative verb and is not used in the continuous form.

items.sentence: We are not agree with the new tax imposed on small traders.
answers: We do not agree with the new tax imposed on small traders.
items.explanation: 'Agree' is a verb, not an adjective; it does not follow 'are'.

items.sentence: My cousin brother works as an engineer at the Tarbela Dam.
answers: My cousin works as an engineer at the Tarbela Dam.
items.explanation: 'Cousin' covers both sexes; 'cousin brother' is a non-standard calque.

items.sentence: It is very hot in here; please on the fan.
answers: It is very hot in here; please switch on the fan.
It is very hot in here; please turn on the fan.
items.explanation: 'On' and 'off' are not verbs; say 'switch on' or 'turn on'.

items.sentence: Please off the lights and the air conditioner before leaving the office.
answers: Please switch off the lights and the air conditioner before leaving the office.
Please turn off the lights and the air conditioner before leaving the office.
items.explanation: 'Off' is not a verb; use 'switch off' or 'turn off'.

items.sentence: The deputy secretary is out of station this week, so the file is pending.
answers: The deputy secretary is out of town this week, so the file is pending.
The deputy secretary is away this week, so the file is pending.
items.explanation: 'Out of station' is a South Asian expression; standard English says 'out of town' or 'away'.

items.sentence: Sir, before we begin the interview, what is your good name?
answers: Sir, before we begin the interview, what is your name?
items.explanation: 'Good name' is a translation of an Urdu/Hindi idiom; standard English simply says 'your name'.

items.sentence: I have received your email and will revert you by tomorrow.
answers: I have received your email and will get back to you by tomorrow.
I have received your email and will reply to you by tomorrow.
items.explanation: 'Revert' means 'return to a former state'; to answer someone is 'reply' or 'get back to'.

items.sentence: Myself Ahmed Raza, and I am applying for the post of assistant director.
answers: I am Ahmed Raza, and I am applying for the post of assistant director.
My name is Ahmed Raza, and I am applying for the post of assistant director.
items.explanation: 'Myself' cannot introduce oneself as a subject; use 'I am' or 'My name is'.

items.sentence: Our principal is very much intelligent and solves problems quickly.
answers: Our principal is very intelligent and solves problems quickly.
items.explanation: 'Very' alone modifies an adjective; 'very much' is used with verbs or comparatives.

items.sentence: The board has decided to prepone the meeting to Monday.
answers: The board has decided to bring the meeting forward to Monday.
The board has decided to bring forward the meeting to Monday.
items.explanation: 'Prepone' is not standard British English; use 'bring forward'.

items.sentence: The updation of voter lists will be completed within two months.
answers: The updating of voter lists will be completed within two months.
The updating of the voter lists will be completed within two months.
items.explanation: 'Updation' is not a standard English word; use 'updating'.

items.sentence: It's important that every adult citizen casts his vote; its a national duty.
answers: It's important that every adult citizen casts his vote; it's a national duty.
items.explanation: 'It's' is the contraction of 'it is'; 'its' is the possessive.

items.sentence: The university has published it's annual report on research output.
answers: The university has published its annual report on research output.
items.explanation: The possessive 'its' has no apostrophe; 'it's' means 'it is'.

items.sentence: Do not loose hope; the results of the interview have not been announced yet.
answers: Do not lose hope; the results of the interview have not been announced yet.
items.explanation: 'Lose' is the verb meaning 'fail to keep'; 'loose' is an adjective meaning 'not tight'.

items.sentence: The screws on this old chair are lose and need to be tightened.
answers: The screws on this old chair are loose and need to be tightened.
items.explanation: 'Loose' (not firmly fixed) is the adjective; 'lose' is a verb.

items.sentence: The prolonged drought has badly effected the wheat crop in southern Punjab.
answers: The prolonged drought has badly affected the wheat crop in southern Punjab.
items.explanation: 'Affect' is the verb meaning 'influence'; 'effect' is usually a noun meaning 'result'.

items.sentence: Rising inflation has a direct affect on the purchasing power of the poor.
answers: Rising inflation has a direct effect on the purchasing power of the poor.
items.explanation: The noun meaning 'result' or 'impact' is 'effect'.

items.sentence: The principle of our college has been awarded the Tamgha-e-Imtiaz.
answers: The principal of our college has been awarded the Tamgha-e-Imtiaz.
items.explanation: 'Principal' is the head of an institution; 'principle' is a rule or belief.

items.sentence: He refused the bribe as a matter of principal, not out of fear.
answers: He refused the bribe as a matter of principle, not out of fear.
items.explanation: 'Principle' means a moral rule; 'principal' means 'main' or 'head'.

items.sentence: The office has run out of stationary, so we cannot print the forms.
answers: The office has run out of stationery, so we cannot print the forms.
items.explanation: 'Stationery' means writing materials; 'stationary' means 'not moving'.

items.sentence: The minister complemented the rescue teams on their swift response.
answers: The minister complimented the rescue teams on their swift response.
items.explanation: 'Compliment' means 'praise'; 'complement' means 'complete or go well with'.

items.sentence: I advice you to read an English newspaper daily to improve your vocabulary.
answers: I advise you to read an English newspaper daily to improve your vocabulary.
items.explanation: 'Advise' (with s) is the verb; 'advice' (with c) is the noun.

items.sentence: My sister practices the violin for an hour every evening.
answers: My sister practises the violin for an hour every evening.
items.explanation: In British English 'practise' is the verb and 'practice' the noun.

items.sentence: All the students passed the test accept Bilal, who was ill.
answers: All the students passed the test except Bilal, who was ill.
items.explanation: 'Except' means 'excluding'; 'accept' means 'receive' or 'agree to'.

items.sentence: Beside English and Urdu, she speaks French and Arabic fluently.
answers: Besides English and Urdu, she speaks French and Arabic fluently.
items.explanation: 'Besides' means 'in addition to'; 'beside' means 'next to'.

items.sentence: He is very economic with his salary and saves something every month.
answers: He is very economical with his salary and saves something every month.
items.explanation: 'Economical' means 'thrifty'; 'economic' relates to the economy.

items.sentence: The Meteorological Department warned of an eminent flood in the Indus.
answers: The Meteorological Department warned of an imminent flood in the Indus.
items.explanation: 'Imminent' means 'about to happen'; 'eminent' means 'distinguished'.

items.sentence: All military personal must report to the parade ground by eight o'clock.
answers: All military personnel must report to the parade ground by eight o'clock.
items.explanation: 'Personnel' means staff; 'personal' means 'private' or 'individual'.

items.sentence: Please keep quite in the reading room of the library.
answers: Please keep quiet in the reading room of the library.
items.explanation: 'Quiet' means 'silent'; 'quite' means 'fairly' or 'completely'.

items.sentence: The Thar Dessert lies in the south-east of Sindh near the Indian border.
answers: The Thar Desert lies in the south-east of Sindh near the Indian border.
items.explanation: A 'desert' is an arid region; a 'dessert' is a sweet dish.

items.sentence: I do not know weather the minister will attend the ceremony.
answers: I do not know whether the minister will attend the ceremony.
items.explanation: 'Whether' introduces alternatives; 'weather' refers to atmospheric conditions.

items.sentence: The doctor told him to lay down and rest for a few hours.
answers: The doctor told him to lie down and rest for a few hours.
items.explanation: 'Lie' (intransitive) means 'recline'; 'lay' (transitive) means 'put something down'.

items.sentence: Could you borrow me your notes on constitutional history for a day?
answers: Could you lend me your notes on constitutional history for a day?
items.explanation: You 'lend' something to someone; you 'borrow' something from someone.

items.sentence: Our English teacher learnt us the rules of punctuation very patiently.
answers: Our English teacher taught us the rules of punctuation very patiently.
items.explanation: A teacher 'teaches' others; the student 'learns'.

items.sentence: The witness said me the whole truth about the incident.
answers: The witness told me the whole truth about the incident.
items.explanation: 'Tell' takes a personal object directly; 'say' does not ('said to me').

items.sentence: The bus fair from Lahore to Faisalabad has gone up again.
answers: The bus fare from Lahore to Faisalabad has gone up again.
items.explanation: 'Fare' is the price of a journey; 'fair' is an adjective or an exhibition.

items.sentence: Who's book is lying on the table in the staff room?
answers: Whose book is lying on the table in the staff room?
items.explanation: 'Whose' is the possessive; 'who's' means 'who is' or 'who has'.

items.sentence: The children left there bags in the corridor and ran to the playground.
answers: The children left their bags in the corridor and ran to the playground.
items.explanation: 'Their' is the possessive pronoun; 'there' refers to place.

items.sentence: Inflation is rising sharply, the poor are suffering the most.
answers: Inflation is rising sharply; the poor are suffering the most.
Inflation is rising sharply, and the poor are suffering the most.
Inflation is rising sharply. The poor are suffering the most.
items.explanation: Two independent clauses cannot be joined by a comma alone; use a semicolon, a full stop or a conjunction.

items.sentence: The paper was very lengthy many candidates could not finish it in time.
answers: The paper was very lengthy; many candidates could not finish it in time.
The paper was very lengthy, so many candidates could not finish it in time.
The paper was very lengthy. Many candidates could not finish it in time.
items.explanation: Two independent clauses fused without punctuation form a run-on; separate or join them properly.

items.sentence: He was seriously ill, therefore he could not appear in the interview.
answers: He was seriously ill; therefore, he could not appear in the interview.
He was seriously ill and therefore could not appear in the interview.
items.explanation: 'Therefore' is a conjunctive adverb, not a conjunction; a comma cannot join the clauses.

items.sentence: The girls hostel at the university was renovated last year.
answers: The girls' hostel at the university was renovated last year.
items.explanation: A plural possessive ending in -s takes an apostrophe after the s: girls'.

items.sentence: My fathers office is on the second floor of the Civil Secretariat.
answers: My father's office is on the second floor of the Civil Secretariat.
items.explanation: A singular possessive needs an apostrophe before the s: father's.

items.sentence: Womens rights are protected under several articles of the Constitution.
answers: Women's rights are protected under several articles of the Constitution.
items.explanation: Irregular plurals not ending in s form the possessive with 's: women's.

items.sentence: Islamabad which is the capital of Pakistan was built as a planned city.
answers: Islamabad, which is the capital of Pakistan, was built as a planned city.
items.explanation: A non-defining relative clause adding extra information must be enclosed in commas.

items.sentence: I wonder whether the train from Quetta will arrive on time?
answers: I wonder whether the train from Quetta will arrive on time.
items.explanation: An indirect question is a statement and ends with a full stop, not a question mark.

items.sentence: Lets meet at the library after the economics lecture.
answers: Let's meet at the library after the economics lecture.
items.explanation: 'Let's' is a contraction of 'let us' and needs an apostrophe.

items.sentence: The job requires honesty, patience and being punctual.
answers: The job requires honesty, patience and punctuality.
items.explanation: Items in a list should share the same grammatical form; here all should be nouns.

items.sentence: The candidate promised better roads, clean water and to build new schools.
answers: The candidate promised better roads, clean water and new schools.
items.explanation: List items must be parallel: three noun phrases, not two nouns and an infinitive.

items.sentence: He is not only intelligent but also works very hard.
answers: He is not only intelligent but also very hard-working.
items.explanation: Elements joined by 'not only… but also' must be of the same type; here two adjectives.

items.sentence: The policy aims at reducing poverty and the improvement of literacy.
answers: The policy aims at reducing poverty and improving literacy.
items.explanation: Coordinated objects of 'at' should both be gerund phrases.

items.sentence: The report was long, detailed and it was very well written.
answers: The report was long, detailed and very well written.
items.explanation: The series should consist of three adjectives without a new clause.

items.sentence: Students should be punctual, polite and work hard.
answers: Students should be punctual, polite and hard-working.
items.explanation: All three complements of 'be' should be adjectives.

items.sentence: The speaker presented his case clearly, confidently and with logic.
answers: The speaker presented his case clearly, confidently and logically.
items.explanation: Items in a series should match; here all three should be adverbs.

items.sentence: She had to choose between staying in Lahore or to move to Karachi.
answers: She had to choose between staying in Lahore and moving to Karachi.
items.explanation: 'Between' pairs with 'and', and both choices should be gerunds.

items.sentence: Walking along Clifton beach, the sunset looked magnificent.
answers: Walking along Clifton beach, we found the sunset magnificent.
As we walked along Clifton beach, the sunset looked magnificent.
items.explanation: The participle must refer to the subject of the main clause; the sunset was not walking.

items.sentence: Being a rainy day, the cricket match was abandoned without a ball bowled.
answers: It being a rainy day, the cricket match was abandoned without a ball bowled.
As it was a rainy day, the cricket match was abandoned without a ball bowled.
items.explanation: The opening phrase has no logical subject; the match was not 'a rainy day'.

items.sentence: While cooking dinner, the electricity suddenly went off.
answers: While I was cooking dinner, the electricity suddenly went off.
items.explanation: The electricity was not cooking; the clause needs its own subject.

items.sentence: At the age of ten, my family moved from Swat to Quetta.
answers: When I was ten, my family moved from Swat to Quetta.
When I was ten years old, my family moved from Swat to Quetta.
items.explanation: The family was not ten years old; supply the intended subject.

items.sentence: I saw a dead snake walking through the garden this morning.
answers: Walking through the garden this morning, I saw a dead snake.
While walking through the garden this morning, I saw a dead snake.
items.explanation: A modifier must be placed next to what it modifies; the dead snake was not walking.

items.sentence: Wanted: a room for a female student with an attached bathroom.
answers: Wanted: a room with an attached bathroom for a female student.
items.explanation: 'With an attached bathroom' describes the room, so it must follow 'room'.

items.sentence: Driving up to Murree, the pine forests took our breath away.
answers: As we drove up to Murree, the pine forests took our breath away.
Driving up to Murree, we were awed by the pine forests.
items.explanation: The forests were not driving; the participle needs a proper subject.

items.sentence: He did a serious mistake in calculating the annual budget.
answers: He made a serious mistake in calculating the annual budget.
items.explanation: In English one 'makes' a mistake, not 'does' one.

items.sentence: Candidates must give full attention to the instructions on the answer sheet.
answers: Candidates must pay full attention to the instructions on the answer sheet.
items.explanation: The standard collocation is 'pay attention'.

items.sentence: She made her homework before going to the tuition centre.
answers: She did her homework before going to the tuition centre.
items.explanation: 'Homework' collocates with 'do', not 'make'.

items.sentence: The government must do serious efforts to control the rising prices.
answers: The government must make serious efforts to control the rising prices.
items.explanation: 'Effort' collocates with 'make'.

items.sentence: The young man did a crime and was arrested by the police.
answers: The young man committed a crime and was arrested by the police.
items.explanation: One 'commits' a crime.

items.sentence: The floods made great damage to the cotton crop in Sindh.
answers: The floods did great damage to the cotton crop in Sindh.
The floods caused great damage to the cotton crop in Sindh.
items.explanation: 'Damage' collocates with 'do' or 'cause', not 'make'.

items.sentence: Strong rain flooded the low-lying streets of Karachi overnight.
answers: Heavy rain flooded the low-lying streets of Karachi overnight.
items.explanation: Rain is described as 'heavy', not 'strong'.

items.sentence: The tourist made a photo of the Faisal Mosque at sunset.
answers: The tourist took a photo of the Faisal Mosque at sunset.
items.explanation: In English one 'takes' a photograph.

items.sentence: Pakistan has done considerable progress in the information technology sector.
answers: Pakistan has made considerable progress in the information technology sector.
items.explanation: 'Progress' collocates with 'make'.

items.sentence: The President did an official visit to China last month.
answers: The President paid an official visit to China last month.
items.explanation: The standard collocation is 'pay a visit'.

items.sentence: He is a man of his words; he will surely keep his promise.
answers: He is a man of his word; he will surely keep his promise.
items.explanation: The idiom is 'a man of his word' (singular).

items.sentence: The ministry approved the funds at the eleventh hours.
answers: The ministry approved the funds at the eleventh hour.
items.explanation: The fixed idiom is 'at the eleventh hour'.

items.sentence: Students preparing for the CSS exam often burn the midnight lamp.
answers: Students preparing for the CSS exam often burn the midnight oil.
items.explanation: The idiom is 'burn the midnight oil'.

items.sentence: His careless remark let the cat out of the box before the official announcement.
answers: His careless remark let the cat out of the bag before the official announcement.
items.explanation: The idiom is 'let the cat out of the bag'.

items.sentence: Such honest officers are found only once in a blue sky.
answers: Such honest officers are found only once in a blue moon.
items.explanation: The idiom is 'once in a blue moon', meaning very rarely.

items.sentence: His provocative statement only added fuel in the fire.
answers: His provocative statement only added fuel to the fire.
items.explanation: The idiom is 'add fuel to the fire'.

items.sentence: The ambulance arrived in the nick of moment and saved the injured man.
answers: The ambulance arrived in the nick of time and saved the injured man.
items.explanation: The idiom is 'in the nick of time'.

items.sentence: The porter carried all our luggages to the platform for fifty rupees.
answers: The porter carried all our luggage to the platform for fifty rupees.
items.explanation: 'Luggage' is uncountable and has no plural form.

items.sentence: The counsellor gave me many useful informations about the admission process.
answers: The counsellor gave me much useful information about the admission process.
The counsellor gave me a lot of useful information about the admission process.
items.explanation: 'Information' is uncountable; it takes no plural and is used with 'much', not 'many'.

items.sentence: We need new furnitures for the conference room before the audit.
answers: We need new furniture for the conference room before the audit.
items.explanation: 'Furniture' is uncountable and is never pluralised.

items.sentence: The sceneries of the Swat Valley attract thousands of tourists every summer.
answers: The scenery of the Swat Valley attracts thousands of tourists every summer.
items.explanation: 'Scenery' is uncountable, so it takes no plural and a singular verb.

items.sentence: He has a lot of works to finish before the end of the month.
answers: He has a lot of work to finish before the end of the month.
items.explanation: 'Work' in the sense of tasks is uncountable; 'works' means artistic creations or a factory.

items.sentence: The police found several evidences against the accused in his house.
answers: The police found several pieces of evidence against the accused in his house.
items.explanation: 'Evidence' is uncountable; count it with 'pieces of'.

items.sentence: She sold all her jewelleries to pay her son's university fees.
answers: She sold all her jewellery to pay her son's university fees.
items.explanation: 'Jewellery' is uncountable and has no plural.

items.sentence: The machineries at the old textile mill are completely outdated.
answers: The machinery at the old textile mill is completely outdated.
items.explanation: 'Machinery' is uncountable, so it takes no plural and a singular verb.

items.sentence: My friend gave me a good news about the result of my interview.
answers: My friend gave me good news about the result of my interview.
My friend gave me a piece of good news about the result of my interview.
items.explanation: 'News' is uncountable and cannot take 'a'; use 'a piece of' if needed.

items.sentence: Several strange phenomenons were observed during the solar eclipse.
answers: Several strange phenomena were observed during the solar eclipse.
items.explanation: The plural of 'phenomenon' is 'phenomena'.

items.sentence: The government has launched a five-years plan for rural electrification.
answers: The government has launched a five-year plan for rural electrification.
items.explanation: A compound adjective before a noun uses the singular: a five-year plan.

items.sentence: Ten thousands people attended the rally at Minar-e-Pakistan.
answers: Ten thousand people attended the rally at Minar-e-Pakistan.
items.explanation: After a definite number, 'thousand', 'hundred' and 'dozen' do not take -s.

items.sentence: Both of his mother-in-laws attended the wedding reception.
answers: Both of his mothers-in-law attended the wedding reception.
items.explanation: In compound nouns of this kind the main noun takes the plural: mothers-in-law.

items.sentence: The energy crisises of the last decade have slowed industrial growth.
answers: The energy crises of the last decade have slowed industrial growth.
items.explanation: The plural of 'crisis' is 'crises'.

items.sentence: The farmer was selling fresh potatos and tomatos at the weekly bazaar.
answers: The farmer was selling fresh potatoes and tomatoes at the weekly bazaar.
items.explanation: Nouns such as 'potato' and 'tomato' form the plural with -es.

items.sentence: The villagers took their sheeps to the hills for grazing in summer.
answers: The villagers took their sheep to the hills for grazing in summer.
items.explanation: 'Sheep' has the same form in the singular and plural.

items.sentence: I don't need no help with filling in this application form.
answers: I don't need any help with filling in this application form.
items.explanation: Two negatives cancel each other; use 'any' after a negative verb.

items.sentence: He hardly never arrives at the office before ten o'clock.
answers: He hardly ever arrives at the office before ten o'clock.
items.explanation: 'Hardly' is already negative in meaning, so it is followed by 'ever', not 'never'.

items.sentence: There isn't nothing more the doctors can do for the patient now.
answers: There isn't anything more the doctors can do for the patient now.
There is nothing more the doctors can do for the patient now.
items.explanation: Use only one negative: 'isn't anything' or 'is nothing'.

items.sentence: My grandmother can't hardly read the small print on medicine bottles.
answers: My grandmother can hardly read the small print on medicine bottles.
items.explanation: 'Hardly' is negative in force and must not be combined with 'not'.

items.sentence: The suspect denied that he had not taken the money from the safe.
answers: The suspect denied that he had taken the money from the safe.
items.explanation: 'Deny' already carries a negative sense, so the 'that' clause should be affirmative.

items.sentence: The labourers worked all day in the heat without no break.
answers: The labourers worked all day in the heat without any break.
The labourers worked all day in the heat without a break.
items.explanation: 'Without' is negative in meaning and is followed by 'any' or 'a', not 'no'.

items.sentence: Scarcely had the bell rung than the students rushed out of the classroom.
answers: Scarcely had the bell rung when the students rushed out of the classroom.
items.explanation: 'Scarcely' and 'hardly' are followed by 'when' (or 'before'), not 'than'.

items.sentence: Hardly had we reached the station than the train started moving.
answers: Hardly had we reached the station when the train started moving.
items.explanation: 'Hardly' pairs with 'when'; 'than' is used only with 'no sooner'.

items.sentence: Hardly I had finished my speech when a member raised an objection.
answers: Hardly had I finished my speech when a member raised an objection.
items.explanation: When 'hardly' opens a sentence, the auxiliary precedes the subject: 'Hardly had I…'.

items.sentence: No sooner the rain stopped than we set out for the Margalla Hills.
answers: No sooner had the rain stopped than we set out for the Margalla Hills.
No sooner did the rain stop than we set out for the Margalla Hills.
items.explanation: Sentence-initial 'no sooner' requires inversion with an auxiliary.

items.sentence: Work hard lest you should not fail in the final examination.
answers: Work hard lest you should fail in the final examination.
Work hard lest you fail in the final examination.
items.explanation: 'Lest' already means 'for fear that', so it must not be followed by 'not'.

items.sentence: Walk carefully on the icy road lest you will slip and fall.
answers: Walk carefully on the icy road lest you should slip and fall.
Walk carefully on the icy road lest you slip and fall.
items.explanation: 'Lest' is followed by 'should' or the bare subjunctive, never 'will'.

items.sentence: He left home early lest he may miss the flight to Skardu.
answers: He left home early lest he should miss the flight to Skardu.
items.explanation: 'Lest' takes 'should', not 'may' or 'might'.

items.sentence: Speak softly in the ward lest you might disturb the patients.
answers: Speak softly in the ward lest you should disturb the patients.
Speak softly in the ward lest you disturb the patients.
items.explanation: After 'lest' use 'should' or the subjunctive, not 'might'.
